en: The Sutra on the Buddha’s Teaching of the Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Yuezhi Country during the Later Han Dynasty.
At that time, the Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the kingdom of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred disciples.

Fifty people, seventy-two nayutas of bodhisattvas, five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, seven thousand upāsakas, five hundred upāsikās, eight hundred thousand devas of the desire realm, seven hundred thousand devas of the form realm, sixty nayutas of devas of the Śubhakṛtsna heaven, and one hundred million Brahmā devas all followed and stayed with the Buddha.
The disciples who possessed supernormal powers of flight and transformation were named:
the Venerable Jñānakoṭi, the Venerable Aśvajit, the Venerable Mahāsthāman, the Venerable Sthavira,
the Venerable Kīrtivardhana, the Venerable Pūrṇabāhu, the Venerable Viraja, and the Venerable Ghoṣila.
The Venerable Paṇḍita-Parṇa, the Venerable Gomaya, the Venerable Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, the Venerable Nadī-Kāśyapa,
the Venerable Gayā-Kāśyapa, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, and the Venerable Bahudhātuka.
The Elder Mahāvaṇija, the Elder Mahātanuka, the Elder Pūrṇamati, the Elder Avivāda,
the Elder Jātismara, the Elder Gambhīradhyānavibuddha,
the Elder Svāgata, the Elder Revata, the Elder Mūḍharāja, and the Elder Gotragupta.
The noble one who resembles a kinsman, the noble one who is a master of the Brāhmaṇa scriptures, the noble one with great desire, the noble one born in a royal palace,
the noble one who has come to inform, the noble one from the Black Mountain, the noble one who is a master of the Kṣatriya scriptures,
and the noble one of vast learning.
Her female disciples were named:

the bhikṣuṇī Mahācintī-gotra, the bhikṣuṇī Māyāvati, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, the bhikṣuṇī Bhūmicālinī, the bhikṣuṇī Bhūmidhāriṇī, the bhikṣuṇī Janmanopasthāyikā-śirorujā, the bhikṣuṇī Subhūti, the bhikṣuṇī Mṛdugātrī, the bhikṣuṇī Śūrasenā, and the bhikṣuṇī Svayaṃprabhā.
The lay devotees were named:

the Elder who Provides Meals for the Solitary, the Elder Peaceful Mind, the Elder Swift Arm, the Elder Fire-Flower, the Elder Good Appearance, the Elder Endowed with Jewels, the Elder of Far-Reaching Fame, the Elder Fragrance that Warding Off Epidemics, the Elder Auspicious Peace, the Elder Bestowing Abundant Jewels, the Elder Joyfully Praising, the Elder Diligent in Giving at Conception, the Elder Providing for Heretics, the Elder Courageously Subduing Enemies, the Elder Jewel Ear-pendant, and the Elder Jewel-Knot.
The female lay disciples were named Jāḍā, Kālī, Dharmasraddhā, Mṛdusumana, Śītalābhiratā, Duḥkhasukhakṣānti, and Priyapriyā upāsikās.
Such people as these were all of one kind—those who had exhausted all defilements and were valiantly pure—and an incalculable multitude gathered together in a great assembly.

At that time, the Buddha sat, contemplating the Right Path; his face was suffused with light of nine colors, manifesting in thousands upon tens of thousands of transformations, the radiance being exceedingly bright and vast.
The worthy Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Why is it that the color and radiance of the Buddha’s face now change and become so exceptionally bright from time to time?"
Now, the radiance of the Buddha’s face consists of hundreds of thousands of colors; its brilliance shines through from top to bottom with such exquisite clarity.

Since I have served the Buddha, I have never before seen the body of the Buddha so majestic and resplendent, nor has it ever been so doubly luminous. I have never seen the light, majesty, and spiritual power of a *Tathāgata*, a *Samyaksaṃbuddha*, as truly radiant, beautiful, and unfailing as it is today. I shall surely call to mind all the Buddhas of the past, those of the future, and those currently residing in other Buddha-fields.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Did various devas come to instruct you, or did various Buddhas instruct you, to cause you to question me?
Or did it arise from your own wisdom?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"There are no devas, nor is there any teaching of the Buddhas. That which I now ask of the Buddha has merely emerged from my own mind and been reported to you."
Whenever a Buddha sits or rises, or when he goes in or out to wherever he may go, regarding whatever he ought to do or whatever he ought to instruct, I immediately know the Buddha’s intention.
"Now it is only because the Buddhas alone have been thinking of one another in succession that their facial complexions have become radiant in such a manner.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, Ānanda!"
If that which is asked is profound, excellent, and wholesome, it will bring about the deliverance of many.

To ask the Buddha is superior to making offerings to the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas of an entire world-system, or bestowing gifts upon the devas, humans, and even the crawling and flying insects for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas—it exceeds this by a hundred thousand million times.
The Buddha said,
"Ānanda! Now you shall deliver and liberate all the devas, kings, people, and even the smallest crawling and flying insects."

The Buddha said, “The Buddha’s majestic spiritual power is exceedingly profound and difficult to withstand; that which you have asked is most deep. You possess a heart of loving-kindness, and out of compassion for the devas and the people, you have come to the Buddha.”
"If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās are truly and greatly virtuous, they shall all cross over [to liberation].
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"It is like the udumbara tree in the world: it bears fruit but has no flowers; only when a Buddha appears in the world do its flowers bloom."

"In this world, it is extremely rare to encounter a Buddha; now that I have become a Buddha and appeared in the world, if there are those of great virtue, intelligence, and a virtuous mind who can anticipate the Buddha's intentions, they shall not serve the Buddha in vain by his side."
"As for what you have now asked, listen well and listen attentively.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"In a kalpa past, long ago, the great assembly was so vast as to be incalculable, boundless and beyond all discussion."
Furthermore, at that time there was a past Buddha named Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata.
Next, there was a Buddha named Prabhāsa.
Next, there was a Buddha named Candrasūryagandha.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Mount Anming (Sumeru).
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Moon-Sun Face.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Free from Dust and Defilement.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Unstained (Anupalipta).
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Like a Dragon, Subduing All Things (Nāga-vaśī-karaṇa).
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Sunlight (Sūryaprabha).
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Mahāsvara-rāja.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Ratnavimalaprabha.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Suvarṇagarbha.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Flame Jewel Light.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Uplifted Ground.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Lapis Lazuli Light.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Sūryacandraprabha.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Sūryanirghoṣa.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Prabhāpuṣpa.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Abhijñāvicaraṇamati-sāgara;
furthermore, there is a Buddha named Abhinandana-prabha;
furthermore, there is a Buddha named Sampanna-ratna-viśuddha.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Prabhā-vinaya;
furthermore, there is a Buddha named Mahā-gandhābhigandha;
furthermore, there is a Buddha named Krodherṣyā-prahāṇa.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Wondrous Beryl and Purple-Golden Radiance.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Mind-Holding Way-Flower Beyond Surpassing.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Accumulated Multitude of Flowers.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Water Moon Light.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Dispeller of All Darkness.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Sunlight Canopy.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Mṛdu Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Dharmamati.
Furthermore, there is a Buddha named Siṃhavikrāntagajendragāmī.
Furthermore, there was a buddha named Lokendra.
Furthermore, there was a buddha named Viśuddhasvara.
Furthermore, there was a buddha named Ajeya.
Furthermore, there was a Buddha named Luyi Xengla who taught for forty-two kalpas in the center; he has already passed away, having become a Buddha during such an eon.

"The hero among those in heaven and on earth, the valiant general within the scriptures, the path, and the Dharma—the Buddha is one whom none can surpass in preaching the sutras and expounding the Way for the sake of the devas and the people of the world."
Upon hearing the Way of the sutra, King Śrīghoṣa was filled with joy and attained understanding; he immediately renounced his royal position to become a bhikṣu named Dharmakāla.
He resolved to attain the mind of a bodhisattva; he was a man of eminent talent, possessing courageous wisdom beyond compare, and was utterly extraordinary among men.
"Having arrived at the place of the Buddha King of Abundant Worldly Sovereignty, he prostrated himself in salutation, knelt with palms joined, and praised the Buddha, saying:
'Your immeasurable radiance and majesty are without limit;
Such blazing brilliance—none can equal it.'"
Whether it be the form of the sun-mani jewel, fire, the moon, or water,
their radiance cannot be reached, and their colors are difficult to compare.
His complexion is beyond measure, the most supreme in all the worlds;
such is his great voice, which pervades countless lands.
Whether through samādhi-concentration, diligence, or wisdom, [he manifests these qualities].
His majestic virtue is peerless, supreme and rare;
With deep, subtle, and true mindfulness, he attains the Buddha-dharma from this.
Holding awakening like the great ocean, its limits have no bottom.
Hatred and delusion—these are absent in the World-Honored One.
Praise be to the Buddha, the Hero of the World; one can never tire of him from beginning to end.
The Buddha is like a fine flowering tree, whom all love and delight in.
Wherever the people see me, all rejoice.
When I attain Buddhahood, I vow that I shall be like the Dharma King,
delivering beings across the cycle of birth and death, so that none remain without liberation.
Generosity tames the mind; so too do ethical discipline, patience, and diligence.
Such is meditative concentration, and wisdom is the supreme among them all.
I vow that upon attaining Buddhahood, may I universally cause all beings to attain these very things.
From all fears, I have attained great peace.
Even if there were hundreds of thousands, billions, and tens of millions of Buddhas—
were the number of such Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, [I would still be secure].
Even if one were to calculate Buddhas as numerous as grains of sand and offer worship to them all,
it would not equal seeking the True Path with steadfast courage and without fear.
It is like the worlds of shifting sands within the waters of the Ganges.
Furthermore, doubling that which is incalculable, throughout countless lands,
his blazing radiance illuminates everything, pervading all these numerous realms;
such power of diligence and majesty are difficult to measure.
May I become a Hero of the World, with a land that is foremost among all;
may my assembly be exceptionally sublime and beautiful, and my place of enlightenment surpass all other realms.
May my land be like the realm of Nirvana, such that there is no equal to it.
I shall always have compassion for them, delivering and liberating all people.
Those who are reborn in the ten directions, their minds joyful and pure,
having already arrived in my land, they dwell in happiness, joy, and peace.
Fortunately, the Buddha has seen and granted me his clear faith; this is my primary witness.
I have made my vow there, through the power of diligence and what I desire.
The World-Honored Ones of the ten directions all possess unimpeded wisdom.
Constantly mindful of this Honored Hero, who knows the conduct of my mind,
may he cause my body to abide firm amidst all bitter poisons;
through the power of my diligent effort, I shall endure them and never regret it.

After the bhikṣu Dharmaguptaka had uttered these praises for the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha King Who Abounds in the World, he resolved his mind to seek the unsurpassed, true, and perfect path of supreme enlightenment, saying:
"I establish this vow:
whatever the Tathāgata possesses, may I obtain it all."
“Uproot the very root of the toil and suffering of birth and death for these people, and cause them all to become like the Buddha.
‘Pray, preach the sutra for us; let that which we may practice lead to swift resolution, so that when I attain Buddhahood, none shall surpass me.’”

"I pray that the Buddha will explain for me the merits of the buddha-fields of all Buddhas; I shall uphold them and dwell therein immediately, and I shall likewise take up the vow to create a buddha-field in such a manner."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“The World-Honored One, King Abundant, knowing that the aspirations of the Bodhisattva Dharmaratnagarbha were lofty, noble, and excellent, immediately preached a sutra for him, saying:

‘Suppose there were the waters of the great ocean, and a single person were to measure them out with a bushel, never ceasing for an entire kalpa; they might still be exhausted until the sea is emptied and its bottom mud revealed.’”
If a person seeks the Way with a sincere heart, how could it be that they do not attain it?
One who pursues it with diligent effort without ceasing will surely obtain whatever they desire within their heart.
When the Bodhisattva Dharmagarbha heard the World-Honored King Buddha preach the sutra in this manner, he was filled with great joy and leaped for gladness.

That Buddha then selected from among the gods and people of two hundred and ten billion buddha-fields those lands that were good or evil, beautiful or ugly, and chose according to the wishes in their hearts to bestow them upon them.

When the World-Honored King of Abundance Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Bodhisattva Treasure-Store of the Dharma concentrated his mind and immediately attained the celestial eye of penetrating vision. He clearly beheld the good and evil of the gods and people, as well as the beauty and ugliness of the lands, within twenty-one billion buddha-fields. Then, selecting what his heart desired and vowed for, he secured these twenty-four vows of the sutra; he upheld and practiced them with diligent effort, fierce valor, and tireless seeking.

Having thus served and made offerings to countless Buddhas over incalculable kalpas, and having encountered past Buddhas also beyond measure, this Bodhisattva Dharma-ratnagarbha subsequently attained Buddhahood for himself, named Wuliang Qingjing Jue Zuizun (Infinite Pure Enlightenment Most Honored One). His wisdom was courageous and fierce, and his radiance was peerless.

The land where I currently reside is most excellent and auspicious; there, in other Buddha-lands throughout the eight directions and the zenith and nadir, I instruct countless devas, humans, and even the wriggling insects of the crawling species, so that none fail to attain transcendence and liberation from sorrow and suffering.

"When the Buddha Amitābha was a bodhisattva, he constantly practiced these twenty-four vows; he cherished and valued them, maintained them with reverence and obedience, and applied himself with diligence to the practice of dhyāna."
"He stands far above the multitude, preeminent and distinct, such that none can equal him.
The Buddha said,
"What are these twenty-four vows?"
"First, when I become a Buddha, may there be no hells, beasts, hungry ghosts, or any kind of crawling and flying insects in my land; only upon obtaining this vow shall I become a Buddha;
if I cannot obtain this vow, I will never become a Buddha."

"Second, when I become a Buddha, may it be that among the people of my land who come to be born in my country, none shall go from my land to be reborn again in the hells, as hungry ghosts, or as crawling insects and beasts;
if there should be those born therein, may I not attain Buddhahood."
"Third, when I become a Buddha, if there are among the people who come to be born in my land any who are not of a single golden hue, may I not attain Buddhahood.
"Fourth, when I become a Buddha, if there are those among the people who come to be born in my land who differ from devas and worldly humans, may I not attain Buddhahood.

"5. When I become a Buddha, if there are people who come to be born in my land and they are unable to all know and recollect the origins and details of where they have come from—their past lives across ten billion kalpas—and if they do not fully know and remember their places of origin, may I not become a Buddha."
"Sixth, when I become a Buddha, if there are people who come to be born in my land and I do not possess the power of universal vision, may I not become a Buddha.
Seventh, when I become a Buddha, if there are people who come to be born in my land and I do not know all that is thought in the minds of others, may I not become a Buddha."
"8. When I become a Buddha, if there are among the people of my land who are not all able to fly, may I not attain Buddhahood.
9. When I become a Buddha, if there are among the people of my land who are not all able to hear with perfect clarity, may I not attain Buddhahood."
"10. When I become a Buddha, if there are those among the people in my land who possess desire and lust, I shall not become a Buddha.
11. When I become a Buddha, if the people dwelling in my land do not all attain parinirvāṇa, I shall not become a Buddha."

"12. When I become a Buddha, may all the gods, humans, and even the wriggling creatures throughout the thousands of billions of Buddha-lands in the eight directions, above and below, become great disciples of the Pratyekabuddhas who serve as my conditions; may they all practice single-minded dhyāna and together count the number of my disciples within my land, remaining thus for ten billion kalpas without anyone being able to count them.
If this is not so, may I not attain Buddhahood."

“Thirteenth: When I become a Buddha, may my radiance surpass that of the sun and moon, exceeding the brilliance of all Buddhas by hundreds of billions of times. May it illuminate the dark and hidden places of countless worlds so that they are always brightly lit. May all devas, humans, and even the smallest crawling creatures who behold my radiance give rise to a heart of compassion, perform wholesome deeds, and be reborn in my land;
if this were not so, I would not become a Buddha.”

"Fourteenth: When I become a Buddha, I shall cause the gods, humans, and even the crawling insects of countless Buddha-lands throughout the eight directions and above and below to attain the fruit of Pratyekabuddha or the realization of a Śrāvaka disciple; and while they sit in meditation with single-minded focus, wishing to calculate and know my lifespan for many thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, may there be none who can know the limit of my life.
If this were not so, I would not become a Buddha."

"15. When I become a Buddha, among the people who come to be born in my land, with the exception of the lifespan desired by the inhabitants of my land, there shall be no one able to calculate the lifespans of the other people;
if it were not so, I would not become a Buddha."
"Sixteenth: When I become a Buddha, may all the people in my land be free from any evil intent;
if this were not so, I would not become a Buddha. Seventeenth:

When I become a Buddha, may my name be heard throughout the eight directions and the ten quarters in countless Buddha-lands. May the various Buddhas each, amidst their assemblies of disciples, praise the excellence of my merits and my land. May the devas, humans, and even the crawling insects who hear my name all leap for joy and come to be reborn in my land."
"If it were not so, I would not become a Buddha. Eighteenth:

When I become a Buddha, among the people of the various Buddha-lands who practice the path of a bodhisattva, they shall constantly mind my pure and clean heart; at the end of their lives, I will fly through the air with an incalculable assembly of bhikṣus to welcome them, standing before them together, so that they immediately return to be born in my land as *avaivartika* [non-retrogressive] ones;
if it were not so, I would not become a Buddha."

"Nineteenth: When I become a Buddha, if the people of other Buddha-lands who have committed evil in previous lives hear my name and, seeking the true path, desire to come and be born in my land, I shall ensure that at the end of their lives they never again fall into the three evil realms, provided this is in accordance with their sincere aspiration;
if it were otherwise, I would not become a Buddha."
"Twenty: When I become a Buddha, the bodhisattvas in my land shall not be limited to those who require only one more birth;
setting aside these other vows and merits, were it otherwise, I would not become a Buddha."
"Twenty-one: When I become a Buddha, if the bodhisattvas in my land do not all possess the thirty-two marks [of a great man], I shall not become a Buddha. Twenty-two:

When I become a Buddha, if the bodhisattvas in my land who wish to travel together to offer worship to the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above, and below, cannot all fly through the air; or if they desire ten thousand kinds of spontaneous objects, which do not all appear before them for them to take and offer to the Buddhas everywhere, and then return to my land before noon on the following day—if this were not so, I would not become a Buddha."

"Twenty-three: When I become a Buddha, whenever the bodhisattvas in my land wish to eat, bowls made of the seven treasures shall spontaneously produce food and drink of a hundred flavors before them; once they have finished eating, the bowls shall all vanish of their own accord.
If it were not so, I would not become a Buddha."
"Twenty-fourth: When I become a Buddha, if the bodhisattvas in my land who preach the sutras and practice the Way do not equal the Buddhas, may I not attain Buddhahood.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"When the Buddha Immeasurable Pure Light was a bodhisattva, he constantly practiced these twenty-four vows: he practiced giving with generosity, did not violate the prohibitions of the Way, cultivated patience and diligence, and maintained single-minded wisdom."
His aspiration was always courageous and fierce; he did not disparage the sutras or the Dharma, seeking them with tireless diligence.

Time and again, he alone renounced his kingdom and abdicated his kingship, severing all ties to wealth and sensual beauty. With refined clarity, he pursued his vows, remaining impartial toward all things, neither favoring nor rejecting.
Having accumulated merit and cultivated virtue for incalculable kalpas, he attained Buddhahood by himself and has fully realized all these qualities, never forgetting his past efforts.
The Buddha said:
“The radiance of the Buddha Immeasurable Purity is most honored, supreme, and peerless; the radiances of all other Buddhas cannot compare to it.”
Among the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above, and below, there are some whose light from the crown of their heads illuminates seven *zhang*;
some whose light from the crown of their heads illuminates one *li*; some whose light from the crown of their heads illuminates five *li*;
some whose light from the crown of their heads illuminates twenty *li*; and some whose light from the crown of their heads...
The radiance shines for forty *li*; among them, the light from the crowns of some Buddhas’ heads shines for eighty *li*;

among them, the light from the crowns of some Buddhas’ heads shines for one hundred and sixty *li*; among them, the light from the crowns of some Buddhas’ heads shines for three hundred and twenty *li*;
among them, the light from the crowns of some Buddhas’ heads shines for six hundred and forty *li*.
There is a Buddha whose radiance from his neck illuminates one thousand three hundred *li*;
there is a Buddha whose radiance from his neck illuminates two thousand six hundred *li*; there is a Buddha whose radiance from his neck illuminates five thousand two hundred *li*;
there is a Buddha whose radiance from his neck illuminates ten thousand four hundred *li*; and there is a Buddha whose radiance from his neck...
The light from one Buddha’s crown illuminates twenty-one thousand li; the light from another Buddha’s crown illuminates forty-two thousand li;
the light from another Buddha’s crown illuminates eighty-four thousand li; the light from another Buddha’s crown illuminates one hundred and seventy thousand li;
and the light from another Buddha’s crown illuminates three hundred and fifty thousand li.
Among them, there was a Buddha whose radiance from his neck illuminated seven hundred thousand *li*;

among them, there was a Buddha whose radiance from his neck illuminated one million five hundred thousand *li*; among them, there was a Buddha whose radiance from his neck illuminated three million *li*;
among them, there was a Buddha whose radiance from his neck illuminated six million *li*; among them, there was a Buddha whose neck...
The radiance shone for one hundred and twenty million *li*.
Among them, the light from the crown of some Buddhas’ heads illuminated one Buddha-land; the light from the crowns of others’ heads illuminated two Buddha-lands;
the light from the crowns of others’ heads illuminated four Buddha-lands; among them, there were [Buddhas whose]...
The light from the neck of one Buddha illuminates eight buddha-fields; the light from the neck of another Buddha illuminates fifteen buddha-fields;
the light from the neck of another Buddha illuminates thirty buddha-fields; the light from the neck of another Buddha illuminates sixty buddha-fields;
and the light from the neck of another Buddha illuminates one hundred and twenty buddha-fields.
Within these lands, there are Buddhas whose light from the crown of their heads illuminates five hundred Buddha-lands;
there are Buddhas whose light from the crown of their heads illuminates a thousand Buddha-lands; there are Buddhas whose light from the crown of their heads illuminates two thousand Buddha-lands;
there are Buddhas whose light from the crown of their heads illuminates four thousand Buddha-lands; and there are Buddhas whose light from the crown of their heads...
The light from the crown of one Buddha’s head illuminates eight thousand buddha-lands; the light from the crown of another Buddha’s head illuminates sixteen thousand buddha-lands;
the light from the crown of another Buddha’s head illuminates thirty-two thousand buddha-lands;
the light from the crown of another Buddha’s head illuminates sixty-four thousand buddha-lands; the light from the crown of another Buddha’s head illuminates thirteen... [thousand buddha-lands].
Among those ten thousand Buddha-lands, there was a Buddha whose light from the crown of his head illuminated two hundred and sixty thousand Buddha-lands;
among them, there was a Buddha whose light from the crown of his head illuminated five hundred thousand Buddha-lands;

among them, there was a Buddha whose light from the crown of his head illuminated one million Buddha-lands; and among them, there was a Buddha whose light from the crown of his head illuminated two million Buddha-lands.
The Buddha said:
"The radiance from the necks of the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above, and below, illuminates all in this same manner;
the flaming radiance from the necks of the immeasurable, pure Buddhas illuminates thousands of myriads of Buddha-lands."
Why is it that the light radiated by the Buddhas has varying distances of reach?

It is because when they were originally seeking the Way as Bodhisattvas in their past lives, the merits of their respective vows differed in magnitude; thus, upon attaining Buddhahood, each obtained exactly what they had vowed, and for this reason, their radiance differs in its extent.
The majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas is equal; they act according to the desires of their sovereign will without prior deliberation.
The light of the Buddha Amitābha’s Radiance is the greatest, such that the lights of all other Buddhas cannot reach it.
The Buddha praised the radiance of the Buddha Amitābha:
"The radiance of the Buddha Amitābha is exceedingly excellent; it is most sublime among all that is good, surpassingly delightful beyond compare, and infinitely extraordinary."
The radiance of the Buddha Amitābha is exceptionally sublime, surpassing the brilliance of the sun and moon by hundreds of billions of times.
The radiance of the Buddha Amitābha is the most brilliant among the radiances of all Buddhas;
the radiance of the Buddha Amitābha is the most excellent among the radiances of all Buddhas.
The light of the Buddha Amitābha is the most heroic among the lights of all Buddhas;
the light of the Buddha Amitābha is the most excellent and auspicious among the lights of all Buddhas;
the light of the Buddha Amitābha is the king among the lights of all Buddhas.
The radiance of the Buddha Amitābha is the most supreme among the radiances of all Buddhas;
the radiance of the Buddha Amitābha is the radiance of infinite longevity among the radiances of all Buddhas.

“The radiance of the Buddha Amitābha shines forth, illuminating the dark and obscure places throughout the countless worlds below, making them perpetually bright. Among all the people and the various species of crawling and flying insects, there are none who do not see the radiance of the Buddha Amitābha; and among those who see his radiance, there are none who do not feel compassion in their hearts and rejoice.”
Among all those in the world who are lustful, wrathful, or deluded, there is none who, upon seeing the light of the Buddha Immeasurable Purity, does not perform wholesome deeds.

In the various hells, among the animals, and in the realms of hungry ghosts where they suffer the torments of interrogation and punishment, when the light of the Buddha Immeasurable Purity reaches them, all their afflictions cease; they can no longer be punished, and after death, there is none who does not attain liberation from sorrow and suffering.

"The radiance of the Buddha Amitābha (Immeasurable Pure Radiance) reaches throughout the eight directions, above and below, extending infinitely and boundlessly across innumerable buddha-fields; there are no devas or humans who do not hear and know of it, and among those who hear and know it, none fail to attain transcendence."
The Buddha said:

"It is not only I who praise the light of the Buddha Immeasurable Purity; the countless Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Arhats of the eight directions, above, and below, all praise it in this same way."
The Buddha said:
"Should there be people—sons of good family or daughters of good family—who hear the name of the Buddha Immeasurable Purity and praise his radiance."

Thus, morning and evening, one should constantly praise its brilliant and beautiful radiance with an uninterrupted and sincere mind. If one desires in one's heart to be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity, one shall be honored by all bodhisattvas and arhats, possessing wisdom and valor.

If he subsequently becomes a Buddha, he too shall likewise be praised for his radiance by countless pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats throughout the eight directions, above and below; it shall be just as this.
When the assembly of bhikṣus, the bodhisattvas, the arhats, the devas, the kings, and the people heard this, they all rejoiced and leaped for joy; there was none who did not offer praise.
The Buddha said:

"The path of my immeasurable, pure Buddha-light is magnificent and beautiful; its lofty renown is most excellent and wholesome, such that even a day and night of an eon would not suffice to exhaust it. I have merely told you this as a brief narrative."
The Buddha declared that the Bodhisattva Wuliangqingjing (Amitābha) had sought and obtained these twenty-four vows.

At that time, Prince Ajātaśatru and five hundred sons of great lay elders (gṛhapati), each holding a golden flowered parasol, came forward to offer them to the Buddha; having done so, they all withdrew to sit to one side to listen to the sutra.

When Prince Ajātaśatru and the five hundred sons of elders heard the twenty-four vows of the Buddha Amitābha, they were all filled with great joy and leaped for gladness; together in their hearts they made this vow:
"When we later become Buddhas, may we all be exactly like the Buddha Amitābha."
The Buddha, knowing this, addressed the community of bhikṣus:
"This Prince Ajātaśatru and the five hundred sons of elders shall, after incalculable kalpas, all become Buddhas, just like the Buddha Amitābha (Immeasurable Pure)."
The Buddha said:

"This Crown Prince Ajātaśatru and these five hundred sons of elders have practiced the path of the bodhisattva for incalculable kalpas; having each made offerings to four hundred billion buddhas, they have now come once more to make offerings to me."

This Crown Prince Ajātaśatru and his five hundred followers were all my disciples during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha in a previous life; they have now gathered together once again by a meeting of karmic affinities.
When the bhikṣu-saṃgha heard the Buddha’s words, their hearts leaped with joy; there was not one who was not filled with gladness.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“Since the Buddha Immeasurable Purity attained Buddhahood, eighteen kalpas have passed. The land where he dwells is named Sukhāvatī, located precisely in the western direction, a distance of ten trillion Sumeru mountains from this realm of Jambudvīpa.”
“The lands of that country are all composed of the seven treasures naturally:

the first treasure is called white silver; the second treasure is called gold; the third treasure is crystal; the fourth treasure is lapis lazuli; the fifth treasure is coral; the sixth treasure is amber; and the seventh treasure is musaragalva.”
These seven treasures all constitute the ground together, vast, expansive, and infinitely great;
they intermingle and penetrate one another, each radiating brilliant light with extreme clarity, naturally soft, exquisite, and beyond compare.

"Just as that ground of the seven treasures is the most refined essence among all the various treasures of the eight directions, above, and below, it is entirely spontaneous, having arisen through the collective transformation of their convergence; those treasures are comparable to the seven treasures of the sixth heaven."
"In that land there is no Mount Sumeru; its sun, moon, stars, and planets, as well as the first Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the second Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, all reside in the void of space."
"In that land there are no great oceans, nor are there small seas; there are no rivers or Ganges waters, nor are there mountains, forests, or valleys; there is not a single place of darkness."

“The land of that country consists entirely of the seven treasures and is perfectly level; it is devoid of hells, birds, beasts, hungry ghosts, and any kind of crawling or flying insects, and it is free from asuras, nāgas, and spirits.”
“There will never be a time of great rain, nor will there be spring, summer, autumn, or winter;
there will be neither extreme cold nor excessive heat, but it will always be temperate and balanced, exceedingly pleasant and incomparably excellent.”

"There are ten thousand kinds of natural objects and foods of a hundred flavors; whatever one desires to obtain appears naturally before them, and whatever one does not desire naturally vanishes away."
For example, like the natural objects of the sixth heaven, which are as spontaneous as nature itself, all things there accord with one's will.
In that land, there are only bodhisattvas and arhats; there are no women, and their lifespan reaches the ultimate limit, lasting for incalculable kalpas.
Those women who attain rebirth there are born by transformation and all become men.

There are immeasurable numbers of bodhisattvas and arhats, all of whom possess the power of clairvoyance and clairaudience—they see one another from afar, gaze upon one another from afar, and hear one another’s voices from afar. All are seekers of the Way who are virtuous; they are of one and the same kind, with no differences among them.
Those bodhisattvas and arhats all had countenances that were upright and handsome, pure and exceptionally beautiful; they were all of one uniform appearance, with none being uneven or ugly.
All these bodhisattvas and arhats are courageous, sharp-witted, and wise.
As for their clothing, they all wear garments that appear spontaneously.

In their hearts, they constantly contemplate the Way and its virtue; whatever they wish to say, their intentions are mutually understood in advance, and in whatever they speak of the Way, they always discourse upon matters of righteousness.
"The bodhisattvas and arhats within that land constantly converse with one another, always speaking of the Way of the sutras and never mentioning the evils of others."
Their speech and voices were like the resonance of three hundred bells; they all held one another in mutual respect and affection, with none harboring hatred.

All spoke according to their seniority and age, their status as superior or inferior, and their order of precedence. They gathered together and conducted themselves with propriety according to righteousness, honoring and serving one another as brothers would.
Treading upon righteousness with benevolence, they do not act recklessly;
their speech is sincere, and they instruct one another in turn;
they do not oppose or conflict with one another, but rather receive and uphold each other's teachings.
Their minds were all pure and clean, free from any longing or attachment; they never possessed lustful desires, thoughts of anger, or states of folly.
They had no perverse thoughts or intentions toward women.
They were all courageous in wisdom, harmonious in mind and joyful, and took delight in the Way of the sutras.

Each knew for themselves their origins from previous lives, as well as the good and evil, survival and extinction throughout billions of kalpas; they also possessed present knowledge that was boundless.

"The lecture halls and monasteries where the Buddha Amitābha provides instruction are all spontaneously formed of the seven treasures—gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, white jade, amber, and musaragalva—which naturally combine with one another to form them; they are exceedingly beautiful and brilliant, surpassingly magnificent beyond compare."
There is no creator, nor is it known from whence it comes;
there is no one who brings it forth, nor is there any place to which it goes.

Because the vows and virtues of the Buddha Amitābha are profound, and because that person has performed wholesome deeds, they are spontaneously born through transformation within the midst of the assemblies where the meanings of the sutras are discussed, the sutras are expounded, and the Path is practiced.

The lecture halls and monasteries were further adorned with towers and railings made of the seven treasures; they were further embellished with necklaces of gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, white jade, amber, and musaragalva, and further draped with networks of white pearls, moon-pearls, and maṇi jewels, which covered them from above.
These all spontaneously produced the five musical tones, the sounds of which were exceedingly beautiful and beyond compare.

"The dwellings of the bodhisattvas and arhats in the Buddha-land of Immeasurable Pure Radiance are all produced through transformation by the seven treasures—gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, musaragalva, and agate—and are mutually formed together."

Their dwellings were each adorned with multi-storied towers and railings made of the seven treasures; furthermore, they were decorated with necklaces of gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, white jade, amber, and giant clam shell, while nets of white pearls, moon-pearls, and maṇi jewels were draped over them, all of which spontaneously produced the five musical tones.

Within the lecture halls, monasteries, and the seven-jeweled residences where the Buddhas of Immeasurable Purity and the various bodhisattvas and arhats dwell, there are natural flowing springs and bathing pools everywhere, both inside and out.
As for those bathing pools, they are all composed of the seven natural treasures—gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and musaragalva—which arise together and mutually form one another.
The sands at the bottom of the water are likewise composed of the seven treasures—gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and musaragalva.
There are pools of pure silver, the sands on their bottoms being all of gold;
among them are pools of pure gold, the sands on their bottoms being all of silver;
and among them are pools of pure crystal, the sands on their bottoms being all of lapis lazuli.
Among them are pools consisting entirely of pure lapis lazuli, the sand at the bottom of whose waters is all crystal;
there are pools consisting entirely of pure coral, the sand at the bottom of whose waters is all amber;
and there are pools consisting entirely of pure amber, the sand at the bottom of whose waters is all coral.
Among them, there are pools consisting entirely of musāragalva, the sand on their bottoms being all of agate;
there are pools consisting entirely of agate, the sand on their bottoms being all of musāragalva;
and there are pools consisting entirely of white jade, the sand on their bottoms being all of purple-golden *cāmīkara*.
Among them, there are pools of pure purple-gold, the sands at the bottom of which are all white jade.
Furthermore, there are pools made of two treasures combined, the sands at the bottom of which are all gold and silver;
furthermore, there are pools made of three treasures combined, the sands at the bottom of which are all gold, silver, and crystal.
Furthermore, among them are some ponds made from four kinds of jewels together: the sand at their bottom consists of gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli.
Furthermore, there are some ponds made from five kinds of jewels together: the sand at their bottom consists entirely of gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, and amber.
Furthermore, there are some ponds made from six kinds of jewels together: the sand at their bottom consists entirely of gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and musaragalva.

Furthermore, among them, there are seven precious substances that together form a single pond; the sand at its bottom consists entirely of gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, musaragalva, and agate.

Within those bathing pools, there are some forty *li* in length; some eighty *li* in length; some one hundred and sixty *li* in length; some three hundred and twenty *li* in length; some six hundred and forty *li* in length; some one thousand two hundred and eighty *li* in length; some two thousand five hundred and sixty *li* in length; some five thousand one hundred and twenty *li* in length; some ten thousand two hundred and forty *li* in length; and some twenty thousand four hundred and eighty *li* in length. Their breadth and width are each equal to their respective lengths.
"This bathing pool is one where all bodhisattvas and arhats constantly bathe.
The Buddha said,
"The bathing pool of the Buddha Immeasurable Purity is forty-eight thousand li in length and forty-eight thousand li in width."

Those bathing pools are all formed by the mutual combination of the seven treasures; the sands at the bottom of those pools are likewise composed of the seven treasures, white pearls, moon-pearls, and maṇi-jewels.

“The water in the bathing pools of the Buddha Amitābha and his bodhisattvas and arhats is entirely pure, fragrant, and clean. Within it are fragrant flowers—specifically, hundreds of kinds of flowers that arise spontaneously, each of various colors and various scents—and every flower has a thousand petals.”
The various flowers are exceedingly fragrant beyond compare; their fragrance is ineffable.
These floral fragrances are not merely the flowers of this world, nor are they surpassed even by the flowers of the heavens.
These floral fragrances arise spontaneously as the very essence among all the floral fragrances of the eight directions, above, and below.
The water flows through the pond, pouring from one place to another;
the flow of the water is neither sluggish nor rapid, and it all spontaneously produces the five musical tones.
The Buddha said:

“The gods, humans, and even the crawling and wriggling creatures from the countless Buddha-lands throughout the eight directions, above and below, who are born in the immeasurable and pure Buddha-lands, are all born by transformation within the lotus flowers of these seven-jeweled water-pools. They then grow naturally and spontaneously, without anyone to nurse them, and all partake of natural food.”

As for their bodies, they are neither the bodies of worldly humans nor the bodies of celestial beings; rather, having accumulated the virtues of manifold good deeds, they have all received natural and void bodies that are exceedingly beautiful beyond compare.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Suppose there were a poor beggar in this world who was made to dwell beside a sovereign emperor; what would that person’s face and physical appearance be like?"
"Would his facial features, appearance, and complexion resemble those of a sovereign?

Ānanda replied, "If this son were to live in the presence of a sovereign, his facial features and form would be exceedingly ugly and unattractive; they would not even equal a hundred thousand billionth part of the beauty of a sovereign’s facial features and appearance."
Why is this? Because he saw that the beggars were so impoverished and exhausted that they had never before tasted fine food.
Having received such poor fare, they could not even eat their fill; they merely took what was offered to sustain their lives, their bones and joints propping each other up.
Having nothing with which to provide for themselves, they are constantly destitute and possess no reserves; they suffer from hunger and cold, trembling with anxiety and grief.

This is solely because in their previous lives, when they were human, they were foolish and lacked wisdom, becoming even more stingy as their wealth increased. Though they possessed riches, they refused to act with compassion, benevolence, or goodness, nor did they practice broad love or charity. They desired only to obtain things for nothing, being greedily attached to food and drink; they ate alone, craving delicacies, and did not believe that giving and lending would be repaid in the future.
Furthermore, they do not believe that performing good deeds will yield blessings in future lives; being muddled and stubborn, they commit even more evils.

Thus, when their lives end and their wealth is exhausted, having been naturally devoid of benevolence and virtue, they have nothing to rely upon. They enter the evil realms and sit amidst suffering, only after this can they emerge and attain liberation.
Having now been born as a human, he was born as a son into a lowly and impoverished household; though possessing a semblance of human form, his appearance was exceedingly ugly.
His clothing was tattered and worn out, leaving him solitary and exposed, unable even to cover his body, living only by begging for alms.
Starving, cold, and suffering in misery, his face was emaciated and weak, unlike that of a human being.
This was the retribution he received for the deeds committed in his previous lives; as the multitude saw him, none felt pity.
Cast away upon the streets, exposed and withered by disease, he was so black, ugly, and utterly loathsome that he could not even be compared to a human.
"Why is it that emperors and kings are uniquely honored and most excellent among men?

It is entirely because in their previous lives and destinies as humans, they performed good deeds, believed in and loved the Way of the scriptures, practiced the virtue of giving, were broadly compassionate and compliant with righteousness, and were kind, benevolent, and delighted in bestowing gifts."
They do not covet food or drink, sharing them with the multitude without any sense of regret or stinginess; thus they remain entirely free from conflict.
Attaining such merit, when their lives end, that virtue follows them, and they shall not fall again into the evil realms.

Having now been born as a human, he was born into a royal family; naturally noble and eminent, he alone rules as sovereign, governing and commanding the people, standing as a preeminent hero among men.
His face and features were pure white, his countenance was gentle and pleasing, and his body was upright; all people together honored and served him.
He enjoyed fine food and exquisite clothing according to his heart's desire, and whatever he wished for in pleasure appeared before him naturally, entirely without conflict or dispute.
"Among human beings, he is handsome and excellent, free from sorrow and full of happiness, and his facial complexion is radiant; it is for this reason that he is thus.
*The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment*, Scroll One.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "If one were to say that this is so—just as a king, though his excellence among men is peerless, if he were to place someone beside a Cakravartin King, that person’s facial features and appearance would seem exceedingly ugly and their form unseemly, being like a beggar standing beside a king."
Even though the face of a sovereign ruler is ugly, it is still surpassed by the exquisite countenance of a Cakravartin king by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.

Just as the Cakravartin is peerlessly handsome throughout the world, were he to dwell beside Śakra, the Lord of the Second Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, his face would be exceedingly ugly and unattractive; it would still be surpassed by the upright and beautiful features of Śakra’s countenance by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.

Just as Śakra, Lord of the Devas, compared to one who dwells in the presence of the Sixth Heavenly King, has a countenance that is exceedingly ugly and unattractive, yet even he is surpassed by the Sixth Heavenly King’s upright and beautiful countenance by hundreds of thousands of billions of times.

Suppose one were to place the King of the Sixth Heaven among the bodhisattvas and arhats dwelling in the Land of Immeasurable Purity; though his face is exceedingly ugly, it would still not equal the upright and beautiful countenances of the bodhisattvas and arhats in the Land of Immeasurable Purity by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of times.
The Buddha said:
“The faces of all the bodhisattvas and arhats of the Buddha Amitābha are entirely upright and exceptionally beautiful, beyond compare, second only to the path of nirvāṇa.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“In the lecture hall, the vihāra, and the residences where the Buddha Amitābha, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats dwell, as well as the inner and outer bathing pools, there are trees made of the seven precious jewels upon them all.”

Among them are trees made entirely of silver, some entirely of gold, some entirely of crystal, some entirely of lapis lazuli, some entirely of white jade, some entirely of coral, some entirely of amber, and some entirely of musāragalva; each of these various kinds stands in its own distinct row.
"Furthermore, among them, there are two kinds of precious substances that together form a single tree:
the silver tree has a silver root, a golden trunk, silver branches, golden leaves, silver flowers, and golden fruit;
the golden tree has a golden root, a silver trunk, golden branches, silver leaves, golden flowers, and silver fruit."
These two kinds of jewel trees mutually complement one another, each forming its own distinct row.
Furthermore, among them are three kinds of jewels combined to form a single tree:
a silver tree with a silver root, a golden trunk, crystal branches, silver leaves, golden blossoms, and crystal fruits;
As for the golden trees, they have golden roots, silver stems, crystal branches, golden leaves, silver flowers, and crystal fruits;
as for the crystal trees, they have crystal roots, silver stems, golden branches, crystal leaves, silver flowers, and golden fruits.
These three kinds of jewel trees revolve together to form a single tree, each within its own distinct row.
Furthermore, there are four jewels combined to form a single tree:
a silver tree with a silver root, a golden trunk, crystal branches, lapis lazuli leaves, silver flowers, and golden fruit.
As for the gold trees, they have roots of gold, stems of silver, branches of crystal, leaves of lapis lazuli, flowers of gold, and fruits of silver.
As for the crystal trees, they have roots of crystal, stems of lapis lazuli, branches of silver, leaves of gold, flowers of crystal, and fruits of lapis lazuli.
As for the lapis lazuli trees, they have roots of lapis lazuli, stems of crystal, branches of gold, leaves of silver, flowers of lapis lazuli, and fruits of crystal.
These four kinds of jewel trees mutually support one another, each standing in its own separate row.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of jewels that together form a single tree:
a silver tree with a silver root, a golden trunk, crystal branches, lapis lazuli leaves, coral flowers, and golden fruit.
As for the gold trees, they have roots of gold, stems of silver, branches of crystal, leaves of lapis lazuli, flowers of coral, and fruits of silver;
as for the crystal trees, they have roots of crystal, stems of lapis lazuli, branches of coral, leaves of silver, flowers of gold, and fruits of lapis lazuli;
as for the lapis lazuli trees, they have roots of lapis lazuli, stems of coral, branches of crystal, leaves of gold, flowers of silver, and fruits of coral.
As for the coral trees, they have roots of coral, stems of lapis lazuli, branches of crystal, leaves of gold, flowers of silver, and fruits of lapis lazuli.
These trees made of the five precious substances mutually support one another, each standing within its own distinct row.
Furthermore, there are trees composed of six treasures together:
the silver tree has a silver root, a golden trunk, crystal branches, lapis lazuli leaves, coral flowers, and amber fruit;
the gold tree has a golden root, a silver trunk, crystal branches, lapis lazuli leaves, amber flowers, and coral fruit.
As for the crystal trees, they have crystal roots, lapis lazuli stems, coral branches, silver leaves, amber flowers, and gold fruits;
the lapis lazuli trees have lapis lazuli roots, coral stems, amber branches, crystal leaves, gold flowers, and silver fruits;
the coral trees have coral roots, amber stems, silver branches, gold leaves, crystal flowers, and lapis lazuli fruits.
As for the agate trees, they have agate roots, coral trunks, golden branches, silver leaves, lapis lazuli flowers, and crystal fruits.
These trees made of the six treasures are mutually formed together, each situated within its own distinct row.
Furthermore, there were trees composed of seven precious substances together:
silver trees with silver roots, golden stems, crystal nodes, lapis lazuli branches, coral leaves, amber flowers, and musaragalva fruits;
and golden trees with golden roots, crystal stems, lapis lazuli nodes, coral branches, amber leaves, musaragalva flowers, and silver fruits.
As for the crystal trees, they have crystal roots, lapis lazuli stems, coral joints, amber branches, musaragalva leaves, white jade blossoms, and gold fruit;
the lapis lazuli trees have lapis lazuli roots, coral stems, amber joints, white jade branches, musaragalva leaves, crystal blossoms, and silver fruit;
the coral trees have coral roots, amber stems, white jade joints, silver branches, moon-pearl leaves, gold blossoms, and crystal fruit.
The amber trees have roots of amber, stems of white jade, joints of coral, branches of lapis lazuli, leaves of conch shell, essence of water, and fruits of gold.
The white jade trees have roots of white jade, stems of conch shell, joints of lapis lazuli, branches of coral, leaves of amber, flowers of gold, and fruits of maṇi jewels.

"These seven-jeweled trees mutually support one another, each arranged in its own distinct row; row after row they meet one another, stem after stem they align with one another, branch after branch they face one another, leaf after leaf they turn toward one another, flower after flower they look upon one another—extremely soft and beautiful—and fruit after fruit they correspond with one another."
The Buddha said:

"In the lecture halls and monasteries of the Buddha Amitābha, there are bathing pools made of the seven treasures both inside and out, surrounded on all sides by trees of the seven treasures; likewise, within the seven-treasure residences of the bodhisattvas and arhats, there are bathing pools of the seven treasures surrounded by rows of seven-treasure trees extending for hundreds and thousands of layers—all of them are exactly like this."
"Each performance produces its own five musical tones, and the sound is exceedingly beautiful beyond compare.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,

"The sounds of the myriad kinds of musical performances of the worldly emperors are not equal to even a single sound from the musical performances of a Cakravartin King, which surpasses them by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of times."

Even the sounds of the ten thousand kinds of musical instruments of a Cakravartin King are not equal to a single sound from the various musical instruments in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, by hundreds of thousands of billions of times.

Even the sounds of the ten thousand kinds of musical performances in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven do not equal even a single sound from the musical performances in the sixth heaven, being inferior by hundreds of thousands of billions of times.

Even the sounds of the ten thousand kinds of celestial music in the sixth heaven do not equal the excellence of a single sound from a tree made of the seven treasures in the Buddha-land of Immeasurable Purity by hundreds of thousands of billions of times.
The Buddha-land of Immeasurable Purity also possesses ten thousand kinds of natural musical performances that are infinite.
When the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, along with the various bodhisattvas and arhats, wishes to bathe, they each enter their own pool made of the seven treasures to bathe.
If the bodhisattvas and arhats wish for the water to submerge their feet, the water then submerges their feet;
if they wish for the water to reach their knees, the water then reaches their knees;
if they wish for the water to reach their waists, the water then reaches their waists.
If he intends for the water to reach his armpits, the water reaches his armpits;
if he intends for the water to reach his neck, the water reaches his neck;
if he intends for the water to pour over his body, the water pours over his body.
"If he intends for the water to turn back again as it was before, the water then turns back and becomes as it was before, according to his every wish and pleasure.
The Buddha said:

"After the Buddha Immeasurable Purity and all the bodhisattvas and arhats have finished bathing, they each sit upon a single lotus flower, whereupon natural turbulent winds arise from the four directions."
As for this turbulent wind, it is neither the wind of the world nor the wind of the heavens;
this turbulent wind is entirely the natural state among all the winds of the eight directions, above, and below, arising through their collective convergence and transformation.
That turbulent wind is neither excessively cold nor excessively warm; it is always harmoniously temperate, its refreshing coolness being beyond compare.
The turbulent wind rises gently, being neither too slow nor too swift, but attaining a perfectly appropriate measure.
The wind blew through the trees made of the seven treasures within the land, and these trees of the seven treasures all spontaneously produced the five musical tones;
the turbulent wind blew the flowers, completely covering the entire land.
The flowers all scattered themselves upon the immeasurable, pure Buddhas, as well as upon the various bodhisattvas and arhats.
As soon as the flowers fell to the ground, they formed a layer four inches thick; they were exceedingly soft and exquisite, beyond compare.
When the flowers begin to wither slightly, natural turbulent winds blow, causing the withered flowers to vanish of their own accord.
Then, again from the four directions, natural turbulent winds arise, blowing upon the trees made of the seven treasures; these trees all spontaneously produce the five musical tones.
The turbulent winds blow upon the flowers, which then naturally scatter over the immeasurable, pure Buddhas, as well as the bodhisattvas and arhats.
When the flowers fall to the ground, natural winds immediately blow them away so that the withered blossoms are all naturally removed.
Then, again, natural winds arise from the four directions, blowing upon the trees of the seven treasures and their flowers; this occurs four times in succession.

"Among the bodhisattvas and arhats, there are those who wish to hear only the sutras, those who wish to hear only the sounds of music, and those who wish to hear only the fragrance of flowers; there are those who do not wish to hear the sutras, those who do not wish to hear the five musical notes, and those who do not wish to hear the fragrance of flowers. Whatever they wish to hear, they immediately hear it alone; whatever they do not wish to hear, they simply do not hear it alone. Thus, all are naturally according to their own will, finding joy in what they desire, never contravening the wishes and aspirations within their hearts."

"After the Buddha Amitābha, along with all the bodhisattvas and arhats, have finished bathing, they each depart. Those bodhisattvas and arhats each follow their own path: among them, some remain on the ground expounding the sūtras; some remain on the ground reciting the sūtras; some remain on the ground explaining the sūtras; some remain on the ground receiving the sūtras orally; some remain on the ground listening to the sūtras; some remain on the ground contemplating the sūtras; some remain on the ground reflecting upon the Way; some remain on the ground practicing single-minded dhyāna; and some remain on the ground practicing the path of the sūtras."

Among them, some were preaching the sutras in mid-air; some were reciting the sutras in mid-air; some were expounding the sutras in mid-air; some were receiving the sutras orally in mid-air; some were listening to the sutras in mid-air; some were contemplating the sutras in mid-air; some were reflecting upon the Way in mid-air; some were practicing seated meditation with single-minded focus in mid-air; and some were walking in meditation in mid-air.

Among them, those who had not yet attained the path of the *srotāpanna* attained the path of the *srotāpanna*; those who had not yet attained the path of the *sakṛdāgāmin* attained the path of the *sakṛdāgāmin*; those who had not yet attained the path of the *anāgāmin* attained the path of the *anāgāmin*; those who had not yet attained the path of the *arhat* attained the path of the *arhat*; and those who had not yet attained the state of an *avaivartika* bodhisattva attained the state of an *avaivartika* bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattvas and Arhats each preached the sutras and practiced the Way; all attained the Way, and there were none who did not rejoice and leap for joy.

Among the Bodhisattvas, there were those who wished to make offerings to the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above, and below. They all came forward together, paid homage to the Buddha Amitābha (Immeasurable Pure), withdrew, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha to take their leave, saying:
"We wish to make offerings to the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above, and below."
The Buddha Amitābha (Immeasurable Pure) then granted his approval, and he sent them to perform offerings for the various bodhisattvas, who all rejoiced greatly.

Thousands of billions of people—countless and beyond calculation, all of whom were courageous and wise—each took flight with their peers in pursuit of one another. Together they flew forth and arrived at the abodes of countless Buddhas throughout the eight directions, above, and below. They all came forward to pay homage to the Buddhas and then made offerings to them.

If those bodhisattvas desire that ten thousand kinds of spontaneous objects appear before them, then there will appear before them a hundred kinds of flowers of various spontaneous colors, a hundred kinds of various spontaneous silken banners and streamers, spontaneous karpāsika garments, spontaneous seven-jeweled treasures, spontaneous lamps and fires, and spontaneous ten thousand kinds of musical performances—all appearing before them.
As for those ten thousand kinds of flowers and fragrances that are spontaneous phenomena, they are neither worldly things nor things of the heavens;
these ten thousand kinds of things are all produced through the natural convergence and transformation of the myriad phenomena throughout the eight directions, above and below.
If they wish to obtain something, it spontaneously manifests before them;
if they do not wish for it, it spontaneously vanishes.

Then all the bodhisattvas together hold offerings and present them to the Buddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats; they circumambulate them on all sides, in front, behind, and around, and whatever they desire in their minds immediately arrives.
At that time, the joy was beyond words.
Whenever the minds of the various bodhisattvas desired forty *li* of flowers, then forty *li* of flowers would naturally appear before them.

All the bodhisattvas together held flowers in the air and scattered them over the Buddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats; the flowers remained suspended in mid-air with their heads pointing downward, exceedingly fragrant and beautiful.
When the flowers slightly wither, they naturally fall to the ground; then, a natural wind blows, and the withered flowers are all spontaneously removed.
If the bodhisattvas each desire eighty *li* of flowers, then naturally eighty *li* of flowers appear before them.
All the bodhisattvas again took flowers together in the air and scattered them over the bodhisattvas and arhats; the flowers all descended toward them while remaining suspended in the air.
When the flowers become small and withered, they fall to the ground of their own accord, and a natural wind blows away the withered blossoms.
If the bodhisattvas each desire flowers extending for one hundred and sixty *li*, then naturally flowers extending for one hundred and sixty *li* appear before them.

All the bodhisattvas then collectively took up flowers in the void and scattered them over the various Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats; the flowers then all descended back down toward the earth from within the void.
When the flowers had slightly withered, they would naturally fall to the ground; then a natural wind would blow, and the flowers would all naturally depart.
If the bodhisattvas each wished for three hundred and twenty *li* of flowers, then naturally three hundred and twenty *li* of flowers would appear before them.

All the bodhisattvas then together took up flowers in the air and scattered them over the Buddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats; the flowers then all descended toward the ground while remaining suspended in the air.
When the flowers slightly wither, they naturally fall to the ground, whereupon a natural wind blows and the flowers are all spontaneously removed.
If the various bodhisattvas each desire to obtain flowers extending for six hundred and forty *li*, then flowers extending for six hundred and forty *li* will spontaneously appear before them.

All the bodhisattvas, moreover, together in the midst of space held flowers and scattered them over the Buddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats; the flowers all descended again toward the earth from within the space.
When the flowers slightly wither, they naturally fall to the ground; then a natural wind blows, and the flowers all naturally depart.
If the bodhisattvas each desire to obtain flowers extending for twelve hundred and eighty *li*, then naturally, flowers extending for twelve hundred and eighty *li* appear before them.

All the bodhisattvas then together held flowers in the air and scattered them over the Buddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats; the flowers all descended toward the ground while remaining suspended in the air.
When the flowers slightly wither, they naturally fall to the ground; then, a natural wind blows, and all the flowers spontaneously depart.
If the various bodhisattvas each desire to obtain flowers extending for two thousand five hundred and sixty li, then flowers of that same extent will spontaneously appear before them.

All the bodhisattvas, moreover, together held flowers in the air and scattered them over the Buddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats; the flowers all descended toward the earth while remaining suspended in mid-air.
When the flowers were slightly withered, they would naturally fall to the ground, and a natural wind would blow so that the flowers would all spontaneously depart.
If the various bodhisattvas each desired five thousand one hundred and twenty li of flowers, then five thousand one hundred and twenty li of flowers would spontaneously appear before them.
All the bodhisattvas then together took up flowers in the air and scattered them over the Buddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats; the flowers all remained suspended in the air, facing downward.
When the flowers slightly wither, they naturally fall to the ground; then a natural wind blows, and the flowers are all spontaneously removed.
If the bodhisattvas each desire flowers extending for twelve hundred and forty *li*, then twelve hundred and forty *li* of flowers will spontaneously appear before them.

All the bodhisattvas, moreover, together in the midst of space held flowers and scattered them over the various Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats; the flowers all descended toward the ground within the space.
When the flowers slightly wither, they naturally fall to the ground; then a natural wind blows, and the flowers naturally depart.
If the bodhisattvas each wish for twenty-four thousand eight hundred *li* of flowers, then twenty-four thousand eight hundred *li* of flowers will naturally appear before them.

All the bodhisattvas, moreover, took flowers from the midst of the sky and scattered them over the Buddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats; the flowers all descended toward the ground while remaining suspended in the sky.
When the flowers slightly withered, they would naturally fall to the ground; then a natural wind would blow, and the flowers would all spontaneously depart.
If the bodhisattvas each desired fifty thousand *li* of flowers, then fifty thousand *li* of flowers would spontaneously appear before them.
All the bodhisattvas, moreover, together in the midst of space, took up flowers and scattered them over the various buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats; the flowers all hung downward in mid-air.
When the flowers slightly wither, they fall to the ground of their own accord; then, a natural wind blows, and the flowers all vanish spontaneously.
If the various bodhisattvas each desire to obtain flowers from a hundred thousand *li* away, then flowers from a hundred thousand *li* away will spontaneously appear before them.
All the bodhisattvas then collectively took up flowers in mid-air and scattered them over the Buddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats; the flowers remained suspended in the air, pointing downward.
When the flowers slightly wither, they naturally fall to the ground; then a natural wind blows, and the flowers all spontaneously depart.
If the bodhisattvas each desire twenty thousand *li* of flowers, then twenty thousand *li* of flowers will spontaneously appear before them.
All the bodhisattvas then collectively held flowers in the void and scattered them over the various buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats; the flowers remained entirely in the void, facing downward.
When the flowers began to slightly wither, they fell to the ground of their own accord; then a natural wind blew, and the flowers all vanished spontaneously.
When the various bodhisattvas each desired forty thousand *li* of flowers, forty thousand *li* of flowers would spontaneously appear before them.
All the bodhisattvas then together took up flowers in the void and scattered them over the various Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and arhats; the flowers all hung downward within the void.
When the flowers slightly wither, they fall to the ground of their own accord; then a natural wind blows, and the flowers all vanish spontaneously.
If the various bodhisattvas each wish to obtain flowers extending eighty thousand *li*, then naturally flowers extending eighty thousand *li* will appear before them.
All the bodhisattvas then together took up flowers in the air and scattered them over the Buddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats; the flowers all hung downward in mid-air.
When the flowers slightly wither, they naturally fall to the ground; then a natural wind blows, and the flowers naturally depart.

If the various bodhisattvas each wish to obtain flowers from a distance of one million six hundred thousand li, then flowers from that distance of one million six hundred thousand li will naturally appear before them.
All the bodhisattvas then collectively took up flowers in mid-air and scattered them over the Buddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats; the flowers remained in the air, facing downward.
When the flowers slightly wither, they fall to the ground of their own accord; then, a natural wind blows, and the flowers all vanish spontaneously.
If the minds of the various bodhisattvas each desire three million *li* of flowers, then three million *li* of flowers will spontaneously appear before them.
All the bodhisattvas, moreover, together held flowers in the air and scattered them over the Buddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats; the flowers all remained in mid-air, facing downward.
When the flowers slightly withered, they would naturally fall to the ground, and a natural wind would blow so that all the flowers would spontaneously depart.
If the bodhisattvas each desired four million *li* of flowers, then four million *li* of flowers would spontaneously appear before them.

The minds and hearts of all the bodhisattvas were filled with great joy and exultation; together in the void, they took up flowers and scattered them over the Buddhas, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats. The flowers spontaneously merged into a single flower, perfectly round and symmetrical on all sides.

The flowers were twice as large as before and exceedingly soft and beautiful; they surpassed the previous flowers in their exquisite beauty, possessing hundreds of thousands of colors, each with a distinct fragrance, so profoundly fragrant as to be beyond description.
All the bodhisattvas were filled with great joy; together in the void, they produced a multitude of sounds as natural music, delighting the Buddha, the bodhisattvas, and the arhats.
At that time, the joy was beyond words.

All the bodhisattvas sat back and listened to the sutra; having finished listening, they all recited it from memory with complete fluency, gaining a deeper understanding of the Way of the sutras and further clarifying their wisdom.
The various flowers and incense that withered slightly fell of their own accord to the ground; then, natural winds blew upon the flowers, causing them all to vanish spontaneously.

Furthermore, from the first heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the thirty-sixth heaven within the Buddha-lands, the bodhisattvas, arhats, devas, and humans all together produced great music and performed various musical arts in the midst of the void.
The various devas who had come forward moved aside to make way for those coming later, and those who came later likewise made offerings as before, each yielding space to the other.
The devas listened to the sutra with joy, all together performing music on a grand scale.
At that time, their joy was boundless.
When the bodhisattvas had finished making offerings and listening to the sutra, they all rose, paid homage to the Buddhas, and departed.

Then he again flew to the abodes of innumerable Buddhas throughout the eight directions, above, and below; there he once more made offerings and listened to the sutras, doing so in full detail for each, just as before.

Thereafter, before noon, all the bodhisattvas would fly away and return to their own lands; they would all go before the Buddha Amitābha to pay him homage and then sit to one side to listen to the sutras.
Having finished listening to the sutra, they were all greatly rejoiced.
The Buddha said:

"When the Buddha Immeasurable Pure Radiance and his bodhisattvas and arhats wish to eat, there spontaneously appear seven-jeweled tables, natural karpāsa cotton garments, and natural woolen rugs to serve as their seats."

When the Buddha Amitābha, along with all the bodhisattvas and arhats, had all taken their seats, there appeared before each of them a natural bowl made of the seven precious substances, within which were naturally present foods and drinks of a hundred flavors.
As for this food and drink, its flavor is unlike that of worldly food and drink, nor is it the flavor of celestial food and drink;

these foods of a hundred flavors are the very essence among all the spontaneous foods of the eight directions, above and below, possessing a fragrance and beauty beyond compare, having arisen entirely through spontaneous transformation.
Their food and drink are at their disposal; whatever flavor they desire, whether sweet or sour, they obtain.

Their alms-bowls are likewise at their disposal; among the bodhisattvas and arhats, some desire silver bowls, some desire gold bowls, some desire crystal bowls, and some desire lapis lazuli bowls. They obtain exactly what they wish for.
Some among them desired coral bowls; some desired amber bowls; some desired white jade bowls;
some desired musaragalva bowls; some desired agate bowls;
some desired bowls made of bright moon pearls; some desired...
As for those who obtain the *maṇi* jewel bowl, if there are those within it who wish to have bowls of purple-polished gold,
all of these are filled therein; food and drink of a hundred flavors arrive at will according to one's desire,
yet they come from nowhere, nor is there anyone who prepares them— they simply manifest spontaneously.
"All the bodhisattvas and arhats eat; their food is neither too much nor too little, being entirely natural and equal.
