When the bodhisattvas and arhats eat, they do not speak of it as good or bad, nor do they rejoice because it is good."
After they had eaten, all the food vessels, bowls, tables, and seats vanished spontaneously;
they would only manifest again when it was time to eat.
The bodhisattvas and arhats were all pure in mind and did not crave food, using it merely for physical sustenance; it all dissolved naturally, being consumed and vanishing away.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“When Amitābha Buddha preaches the Dharma for the bodhisattvas and arhats, they all assemble together in the great lecture hall.”

The bodhisattvas, arhats, devas, and people of that land were so numerous as to be beyond all calculation; they all flew to the abode of the Buddha Amitābha (Immeasurable Purity) and, having approached, paid homage to the Buddha Amitābha before withdrawing to sit and listen to the sutra.

The Buddha Amitābha then extensively expounded the Great Sūtra of the Path and Wisdom to the assembly of bhikṣus, bodhisattvas, arhats, devas, and humans; all heard and understood the path of the sūtra, and there was none who did not rejoice with leaping joy and attain the opening and liberation of their minds.

"Then, naturally, turbulent winds arose from the four directions, blowing upon the trees made of the seven treasures within the kingdom. These trees of the seven treasures all produced the sounds of the five musical notes.
The turbulent winds blew upon the flowers of the seven treasures, and these flowers covered the kingdom, all falling downward into the midst of the void."
The flowers were exceedingly fragrant and exceptionally soft and beautiful; their scent pervaded the entire kingdom.
The flowers spontaneously scattered over the immeasurable, pure Buddhas, as well as upon the bodhisattvas and arhats.
The flowers that fell to the ground were all four inches thick; as soon as they slightly withered, a natural turbulent wind would blow, causing the withered flowers to vanish of their own accord.

Then, from all four directions, natural turbulent winds would arise and blow upon the trees made of the seven treasures, and these trees of the seven treasures would all spontaneously produce the five musical tones.
A turbulent wind blew upon the flowers of the seven-jeweled trees; the flowers, as before, spontaneously scattered over the immeasurable, pure Buddhas, as well as the bodhisattvas and arhats.
The flowers that fell upon the ground were four inches thick; when the flowers began to wither slightly, a natural wind would blow, causing all the withered flowers to vanish spontaneously.
This natural wind blew away the flowers in this manner four times.
Then the devas of the first Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the devas of the second Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
the devas of the third Heaven, the devas of the fourth Heaven,
the devas of the fifth Heaven, the devas of the sixth Heaven, and the devas of the seventh Brahmā Heaven—
From humans up to the devas of the sixteenth heaven, and up to the devas of the thirty-sixth heaven,
all brought ten thousand kinds of natural celestial objects— hundreds of varieties of multicolored flowers,
hundreds of varieties of blended fragrances, hundreds of varieties of multicolored silks, and hundreds of varieties of karpāsa cotton garments.
— Ten thousand kinds of music and performance, each more exquisite and superior than the last, were brought down one by one;
they prostrated before the Buddha Amitābha and thereby made offerings to the Buddha Amitābha, as well as to the various bodhisattvas and arhats.
All the devas and humans again performed great musical performances to delight the Buddha Amitābha, the various bodhisattvas, and the arhats.
At that time, the joy was beyond words.
The various devas and humans who had arrived previously moved aside to make way for those arriving later; those arriving later likewise made offerings as before, each yielding space to the other.

Thus, from the countless Buddha-lands of the eastern direction—immeasurable like the sands flowing along the banks of the Ganges, with one Buddha for every grain of sand—each Buddha dispatched immeasurable and incalculable bodhisattvas. They all flew to the place of the Buddha Amitābha (Immeasurable Pure One), prostrated themselves before him by touching their heads and faces to his feet, and then withdrew to sit to one side to listen to the sutra.
When they had finished listening to the sutra, all the bodhisattvas were filled with great joy; they all rose and paid homage to the Buddha Amitābha before departing.

Furthermore, from the innumerable buddha-fields of the western direction—just as there are grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges River, with one buddha for every grain of sand—each of those buddhas dispatched innumerable, incalculable bodhisattvas. They all flew to the presence of the Buddha Amitābha, prostrated themselves before the Buddha Amitābha by touching their heads to his feet, and then withdrew to sit to one side to listen to the sutra.
When the recitation of the sutra was finished, all the bodhisattvas were filled with great joy; they rose, paid homage to the Buddha Amitābha (Immeasurable Purity), and departed.

Then, from the countless buddha-lands of the northern direction—just as there are grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges River, with one buddha for every grain of sand, their number being thus immense—each of those buddhas dispatched countless, incalculable bodhisattvas. They all flew to the place where the Buddha Amitābha was, came forward to pay homage to the Buddha Amitābha, touched their heads to his feet, and then withdrew to sit to one side to listen to the sutra.
When the recitation of the sutra was finished, all the bodhisattvas were filled with great joy; they rose, paid homage to the Buddha Amitābha (Immeasurable Purity), and departed.

From the south, there were countless buddha-lands—as numerous as the grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges River, with one buddha for every grain of sand—and from each of these lands, the buddhas respectively dispatched countless, incalculable numbers of bodhisattvas. They all flew to the abode of the Buddha Amitābha, whereupon they came forward, paid homage to the Buddha Amitābha, and departed.

Furthermore, in the four corners, there were infinite Buddha-lands—each as numerous as the grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges River, with one Buddha for every grain of sand, their number being exactly thus. Each of these Buddhas dispatched an incalculable and immeasurable multitude of bodhisattvas, all of whom flew to the abode of the Buddha Amitābha (Immeasurable Purity). Having arrived, they prostrated themselves before the Buddha Amitābha, touching their heads to his feet, and then withdrew to sit to one side to listen to the sutra.
When they had finished listening to the sutra, all the bodhisattvas were filled with great joy; they rose, paid homage to the Buddha Amitābha (Immeasurable Pure), and departed.
The Buddha said:

"The countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above, and below have each dispatched their bodhisattvas to fly to the abode of the Buddha Amitābha to listen to the sutra and make offerings, taking turns to vacate one another’s places."

"In this way, there are innumerable Buddha-lands in the eight directions below—each direction being as numerous as the sands along the banks of the Ganges River, with one Buddha for every grain of sand, their number likewise beyond measure—and each of these Buddhas has dispatched innumerable Bodhisattvas, so vast they can no longer be calculated, all of whom fly to the abode of the Buddha Immeasurable Purity. They come before Amitābha Buddha to pay him homage, touching their heads and faces to his feet, and then all withdraw to sit and listen to the sutra."
When the recitation of the sutra was finished, all the bodhisattvas were filled with great joy; they rose, paid homage to the Buddha Immeasurable Purity, and departed.

The buddhas of the upper direction further dispatched various bodhisattvas to fly to the abode of the Buddha Immeasurable Purity to listen to the sutra and make offerings. They took turns opening the way for one another: those who had come first would depart to make way for those who came later, and those who arrived later made offerings in the same manner; thus it continued without ceasing until the very end.
"Just as there are lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, so too are the Buddha-fields in the eastern direction;
from each, bodhisattvas are sent forth to prostrate and pay homage to the Immeasurable Awakened One.
It is the same for the west, south, and north—all such lands, numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges."
These Bodhisattvas sent by the Buddhas prostrate in homage to the One of Infinite Awakening.
These Bodhisattvas from the ten directions fly forth,
all carrying baskets of various flowers and divine silks of many kinds, going to make offerings to the One of Infinite Awakening.
All the bodhisattvas gathered in great assembly, prostrated and paid homage to the Boundless Light;
they circumambulated him three times with palms joined, standing reverently as they extolled the World-Honored One’s immeasurable awakening.
All held flowers and scattered them over the Buddha; with pure minds, they praised him as immeasurable.
Standing before the Buddha, they spoke of themselves:
"May our buddha-fields be like this."
The scattered flowers stayed suspended in the void, merging to form a canopy a hundred yojanas across;
its handle was exquisitely adorned, completely covering the entire assembly.
All the bodhisattvas have gone there; those noble lands are difficult to encounter.
Those who hear the name of the Buddha thus obtain great benefit with swift peace and security.
We and our peers have attained this virtue; all these lands have obtained what they desired.
Considering our own lands as if they were a dream, we have purified this realm for countless eons.
Beholding the Bodhisattvas surrounding the World-Honored One, Whose majestic power is fierce and whose lifespan is infinite,
The assembly of awakened ones in his land is exceedingly pure, Having practiced for inconceivable numbers of eons.
At that time, the World-Honored One of Immeasurable Life smiled;
thirty-six billion nayutas of rays of light issued from his mouth, illuminating all countless lands.
Then the light turned back and circled the Buddha three times before entering through the crown of his head;
its radiance suddenly vanished, and both gods and humans were filled with joy.
Upāli rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bowed his head in prostration,
and asked the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason do you smile?"
May the World-Honored One speak these words of mind;
may he grant me the prophecy of primordial emptiness, and through his compassionate protection, may I perfect the marks of a hundred merits.
All who hear these various sounds shall leap for joy.
The voice of Brahmā and the sound of thunder—these eight kinds of voices are deep and resonant.
The Buddha bestowed upon Pūrṇa this prediction:
"Now I shall speak; you, virtuous one, listen attentively."
The bodhisattvas from all the various worlds arrive at Sūkhāvatī to pay homage to the Buddha;
hearing [the Dharma], they rejoice and practice it extensively, swiftly attaining the pure realm.
Having arrived in this adorned and pure land, one swiftly attains the superknowledges;
with eyes that see through and ears that hear across, one likewise regains the knowledge of past lives.
The Buddha of Immeasurable Enlightenment bestowed upon me this prediction:
"In my past lives I made a fundamental vow that all people who hear me preach the Dharma shall quickly come to be born in my land."
All that I have wished for is now fully realized; those who have come from various lands to be born here have all arrived in this place, attaining the stage of non-retrogression in a single lifetime.
If a bodhisattva further arouses the vow, desiring to make their land like my own realm,
and also keeps in mind the deliverance of all people, causing each to fulfill their vows throughout the ten directions.
Swiftly and easily they shall reach the world-realm of the Land of Peace and Bliss,
arriving at the land of Immeasurable Radiance to make offerings to countless Buddhas.
Having served hundreds of millions of Buddhas, manifesting transformations that pervaded all lands,
and having departed with joy after paying his respects, he returned once more to Sūmadhatī.
Those who do not possess such merit cannot hear the name of this sutra;
only those with pure precepts shall attain the hearing of this True Dharma.
Having once beheld the World-Honored One, the Hero, one gains faith in this matter;
with humility and reverence, hearing and practicing his teachings, one then leaps for joy with great delight.
Those who are evil, arrogant, and slothful find it difficult to have faith in this Dharma;
those who have seen Buddhas in past lives delight in hearing the teachings of the World-Honored One.
It is like one born blind and in darkness who wishes to find a guide for the journey;
if even the śrāvakas are entirely deluded regarding the Mahāyāna, how much more so the worldly commoners?
The God among Gods knows the minds of others; the śrāvakas do not comprehend the Buddha’s conduct, nor do the pratyekabuddhas;
only the Solitary Perfectly Awakened One knows this.
Even if all beings were to become Buddhas, their pure wisdom would know that the source is empty;
even after passing through billions of kalpas, no one could equal the Buddha’s wisdom.

Though one were to discourse and explain for incalculable eons, exhausting one's entire lifespan, one would still not know the Buddha’s wisdom, which is without limit or boundary; such is attained through the practice of purity.
He who honors my teaching and believes in it, Only such a person can understand and comprehend;
One who can receive all that the Buddha has spoken— This indeed is the foremost realization.
Human life is rarely obtained; a Buddha appearing in the world is extremely difficult to encounter.
Faith and wisdom are not easily attained, yet they can be realized if one hears and sees [the Dharma] and strives with diligence.
Hearing this Dharma and not forgetting it, one immediately perceives respect and attains great joy;
such is my virtuous and close kinship, and for this reason, I have resolved upon the path.

Even if the entire world were filled with fire, one should cross through it to hear the Dharma; for one will surely become a leader of World-Honored Ones, delivering all beings from birth, old age, and death.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

“When the Buddha Amitābha has finished preaching the sutra for the sake of the bodhisattvas and arhats, among the devas and humans, those who had not yet attained the stage of srotāpanna shall attain the stage of srotāpanna; those who had not yet attained the stage of sakṛdāgāmin shall attain the stage of sakṛdāgāmin; those who had not yet attained the stage of anāgāmin shall attain the stage of anāgāmin; those who had not yet attained the stage of arhat shall attain the stage of arhat; and those who had not yet attained the stage of avaivartika bodhisattva shall attain the stage of avaivartika bodhisattva.”

Amitābha Buddha immediately accords with their original past lives and the magnitude of the aspirations and preferences of their hearts when they sought the Way; according to their inclinations, he preaches the sutras and bestows them upon them, causing them to quickly attain awakening and realize the Way, so that all possess clear wisdom.

Each person, delighting in the sūtras and the Way they aspire to, finds no lack of joy in reciting and practicing them; thus, each shall chant and recite the sūtras and the Way, mastering them with tireless and boundless proficiency.
Among the bodhisattvas and arhats, there were those who recited the sutras, their voices like the sound of thunder;
among them were those who expounded the sutras, like a swift wind and torrential rain.
At that time, the various bodhisattvas and arhats preached the sutras and practiced the Way, each in this manner, until the end of an entire kalpa without ever experiencing weariness or fatigue.
They were all possessed of wisdom and valor; their bodies were entirely light, and they never experienced any sensation of pain or itching.

At all times, whether walking, sitting, or rising, he was entirely skillful, capable, and courageous—like the king of lions in the deep forest when he has a destination to reach; at such a time, none dare to oppose him.

“The bodhisattvas and arhats in the Land of Immeasurable Purity preach the sutras and practice the Way with such vigor that they harbor no thoughts of doubt or difficulty; their mental activities are hundreds of thousands of millions of times beyond calculation, and they are like the king of the fierce lions.”

Even a hundred thousand ten-thousand million times as many of such fierce lion-kings would still not equal my second disciple, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, by a hundred thousand ten-thousand million times in terms of his valor and ferocity.
"The bodhisattvas and arhats in the Land of Immeasurable Purity all surpass my second disciple, Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
The Buddha said,
"Just as Mahāmaudgalyāyana is courageous and peerless among all the arhats in all the buddha-fields,"

Suppose one were to take the combined wisdom, valor, clairvoyance, and clairaudience of Mahāmaudgalyāyana—his ability to fly and move at will, his knowledge of the eight directions, above and below, and of all matters past, future, and present—and multiply this by hundreds of thousands of billions of times to form a single instance of wisdom, valor, and power; even such a being, when compared to a single Arhat in the Land of Immeasurable Purity, would still fall short of that Arhat’s wisdom, valor, and power by a factor of hundreds of thousands of billions of times.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva among those seated, named Ajita Bodhisattva.
Ajita Bodhisattva rose, knelt with his palms joined, and asked the Buddha:
"In the land of Amitābha Buddha, do any of the arhats ever pass into parinirvāṇa?"
"I wish to hear it.
The Buddha told Ajita Bodhisattva:
"If you wish to know, do you see the stars in these four continents?"
The Bodhisattva Ajita said,
"Indeed, I see them all. The Buddha said:
"And my second disciple, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, flies throughout the four continents; in a single day and night, he travels everywhere to count the stars, knowing exactly how many there are."

In this way, the stars in the four continents are exceedingly numerous and cannot be calculated; yet [the stars in] even a hundred thousand billion times these four continents are still surpassed by this.
The Buddha said, "Suppose one were to remove a single drop of water from the great ocean of the world; would it be possible to cause the ocean water to decrease thereby?
Bodhisattva Ajita replied:
"If one were to remove hundreds of thousands of billions of *dou* and *shi* of water from the great ocean, it still could not cause the sea to diminish.

The Buddha said, "Even if some among the arhats in the land of Amitābha Buddha were to pass into *parinirvāṇa*, it would be like removing a single drop of water from such a great ocean; it could not cause those remaining arhats to be diminished or known as fewer."
The Buddha said,
"If one were to remove the water of a single mountain stream from the great ocean, would it be able to diminish the ocean?
Ajita Bodhisattva replied:

"Just as removing hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of mountain streams from the great ocean cannot cause the ocean water to diminish enough to be perceived as less," the Buddha said, "so too,

when Arhats in the land of Amitābha Buddha pass into parinirvāṇa, it is like removing a single mountain stream from such a great ocean; it cannot cause those remaining Arhats to perceive a reduction."
The Buddha said,
"If one *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [measure] of water were removed from the great ocean, would it be possible to diminish the waters of the sea?
Ajita Bodhisattva replied:

"Even if one were to remove from the waters of the great ocean as many *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (sands of the Ganges) as there are hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of such rivers, it would still not be possible to diminish the waters of the great ocean so that their reduction could be perceived.
The Buddha said:

"In the land of Amitābha Buddha, although the number of arhats who have entered parinirvāṇa is incalculable, and the number of those currently remaining or who have newly attained arhatship is likewise incalculable, there is in total neither increase nor decrease."
The Buddha said:
"Suppose all the waters in the world were to flow together into the great ocean; would this cause the seawater to increase?
Ajita Bodhisattva replied:
"It cannot cause the waters of the sea to increase.
Why is this? It is because the great ocean is the sovereign among all the waters and virtues of the world; therefore, it is able to do so."
The Buddha said:

"The Land of Immeasurable Pure Radiance is also like this. It causes the countless Buddha-lands of the eight directions and above and below, as well as the countless devas, humans, and all classes of wriggling and flying creatures, to be reborn entirely in the Land of Immeasurable Pure Radiance. Although these multitudes are exceedingly great and numerous beyond calculation, the bodhisattvas, arhats, and the assembly of bhikṣus in the Land of Immeasurable Pure Radiance remain exactly as they were before; there is no change in their single Dharma, nor is there any increase."

Why is this? Because the Land of Immeasurable Purity is the most supreme; among the countless Buddha-lands of the eight directions, above, and below, and among the multitudes of bodhisattvas, it is the sovereign.
The Land of Immeasurable Purity is [the foremost] among all those countless [realms].
The Buddha-land is the preeminent land among all Buddha-lands; the Land of Immeasurable Purity is a treasure among the countless Buddha-lands;
the Land of Immeasurable Purity is the most enduring among the countless Buddha-lands;
the Land of Immeasurable Purity is [the foremost] among all the countless Buddha-lands.
The multitude of its sages is preeminent; the Buddha-land of Immeasurable Purity is the most vast among all the countless Buddha-lands;
the Buddha-land of Immeasurable Purity is the most spontaneously natural and unconditioned among all the countless Buddha-lands;
and the Buddha-land of Immeasurable Purity is the most swift, brilliant, excellent, and supremely blissful.
It is infinite.
Why is the Land of Immeasurable Purity and Clarity so uniquely superior?

It is simply because when he was originally a bodhisattva seeking the Way, his vows were courageous and fierce, and he practiced with diligence and without slackening; it is the result of the accumulation of merit that it has become thus.
The Bodhisattva Ajita was greatly rejoiced; kneeling with palms joined, he said:

"The Buddha has spoken of the Land of Immeasurable Purity, where the Arhats who have entered Parinirvāṇa are exceedingly numerous, and where the lands are infinitely vast, supremely blissful and virtuous, bright, beautiful, and peerless—is it truly only thus?"
The Buddha said:
"Among the seven-jeweled residences where the bodhisattvas and arhats of the Land of Immeasurable Purity reside, some dwell in mid-air while others dwell upon the ground."
If one has the intention to cause the dwelling to be the highest, the dwelling shall be high;
if one has the intention to cause the dwelling to be the largest, the dwelling shall be large;
if one has the intention to cause the dwelling to be in the midst of space, the dwelling shall be in the midst of space.
All things naturally follow one's will in whatever actions are performed.
Among them, there are some that cannot be made to function according to one's will within their dwellings. Why is this so?

Among them, those who are able [to attain it] all did so because in their past lives, while seeking the Way, they practiced compassion and diligence, performed many good deeds, and possessed the weight of virtue necessary to achieve it;

those among them who are unable to attain it all did so because in their past lives, while seeking the Way, they lacked compassion and diligence, performed few good deeds, and possessed little virtue.

Each attains these spontaneously; the robes they wear, their food and drink, are all equally provided by nature. It is for this reason that they appear different, so that the multitude may perceive the distinctions in their virtues—their greatness and smallness—and recognize their respective courage and vigor.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Ajita:
"Do you see this abode of the Heavenly King on the sixth heaven?
The Bodhisattva Ajita replied:
“Yes, indeed, I see them all.
The Buddha said,
“The lecture halls and residences of the Land of Immeasurable Purity are hundreds of thousands of millions of times more magnificent than the dwelling place of the Sixth Heavenly King.”
"In the Land of Immeasurable Pure Radiance, all its bodhisattvas and arhats possess the power of clairvoyant vision and clairaudience;
they fully perceive and know all matters of the eight directions, above and below, past, future, and present.

Furthermore, they know the minds and thoughts—both good and evil—of the countless beings in the heavens above and the world below, including all humans and even the smallest crawling insects, as well as everything they intend to say with their mouths."
They all know in which year and which kalpa they shall attain liberation and obtain the human path; they know that they shall be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity;
they know that they shall practice the bodhisattva path or attain the path of an arhat—all these things they know in advance.
"The bodhisattvas and arhats in the Land of Immeasurable Purity all possess their own radiance from the necks upward, and the extent of what they illuminate varies."

"Among those bodhisattvas, there were two most honored bodhisattvas who constantly sat in attendance at the left and right sides of the Buddha Amitābha, attending to his affairs and engaging in discourse.
The Buddha Amitābha would always sit facing these two bodhisattvas, deliberating upon matters of the eight directions, above and below, as well as the past, future, and present."

If the Buddha Amitābha wishes to cause these two bodhisattvas to reach the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above, and below, those two bodhisattvas will then fly and arrive at the abodes of the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above, and below;
wherever they wish to go according to their hearts' desire, those two bodhisattvas will both fly together, arriving with a speed as swift as a Buddha’s, possessing incomparable valor and vigor.
"One of those bodhisattvas was named Pūrṇa, and the other was named Mahānāman; their radiance and wisdom were supreme.

From the radiance on the necks of these two bodhisattvas, a blazing light constantly and brilliantly illuminated the Buddha-lands of a thousand Mount Sumerus in other directions. The radiance from the necks of the other bodhisattvas each illuminated ten billion *li*, while the radiance from the necks of the arhats each illuminated seven *zhang*."
The Buddha said:

"If there are people in the world—sons of good family or daughters of good family—who encounter sudden peril and fear, or who fall into legal trouble with government officials, they need only take refuge in this Bodhisattva Aparājita; there is nothing they shall not attain liberation from."
The Sutra on the Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Two.
The Sutra on the Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhi Loujiachen of the Yuezhi Kingdom during the Later Han Dynasty.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Ajita: "The light from the crown of the head of the Buddha Immeasurable Pure Light is exceedingly brilliant.
The sun, moon, and stars all abide in the void; they no longer revolve or circulate, nor do they possess any luster, for their brightness is entirely eclipsed and no longer appears."

The radiance of the Buddha Amitābha illuminates his land and shines upon other buddha-fields, remaining perpetually bright; it never reaches a time of darkness. In that land, there is no such thing as one day or two days;

there are no fifteen days or one month; there are no five months or ten months; there are no five years or ten years; there are no one hundred years or one thousand years; there are no ten thousand years, one hundred million years, ten billion years, or one hundred billion years; and there are no ten trillion years.

There is not a single kalpa, nor ten kalpas; there are not a hundred kalpas, nor a thousand kalpas; there are not ten thousand kalpas, nor a hundred thousand kalpas; there are not a million kalpas, nor a hundred thousand billion kalpas.
The Buddha said:
"The radiance of the Buddha Amitābha is boundless; his radiance is infinite.

After immeasurable kalpas, after countless kalpas, again after countless kalpas, after countless kalpas, and after kalpas beyond reckoning—throughout these incalculable kalpas—there will never come a time when it becomes dark."
"The Land of Immeasurable Purity and its various devas shall never suffer destruction. Why is this?
Because the lifespan of the Buddha Immeasurable Purity is exceedingly long and his land is most excellent; therefore, it is able to remain so."
The Buddha said:
“The lifespan of the Honored One, the Buddha Immeasurable Purity, shall remain constant and infinite for countless kalpas after his passing; there will be no time of his parinirvāṇa.

While the Buddha Immeasurable Purity teaches in this world, he intends to deliver all the gods, humans, and even the crawling and flying insects of the immeasurable Buddha-lands throughout the eight directions and above and below, desiring that they all be reborn in his land and cause them all to attain the Way of Nirvana.”
All those who act as bodhisattvas desire that all beings become Buddhas, and having become Buddhas, they cause them all to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, they instruct the devas, humans, and even the wriggling and crawling creatures of the eight directions, above and below, desiring that they all likewise attain Buddhahood;
when they have become Buddhas, they in turn instruct countless devas, humans, and wriggling and crawling creatures, causing them all to attain the path of Nirvana and depart.

Those disciples who are to be instructed shall, in turn, instruct one another and successively deliver one another, until they cause them to attain the fruits of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, *arhat*, and the path of a *pratyekabuddha*.
In this way, they all successively deliver one another and attain the Way of Nirvāṇa; yet the Buddha Amitābha remains eternally and has no desire to enter Parinirvāṇa.

Through the successive deliverances of the Buddha Amitābha, beings continue in this manner for countless kalpas, for countless kalpas, and for kalpas beyond reckoning, such that there will never be a time when he enters Parinirvāṇa.
The gods, humans, insects, and all crawling creatures from the eight directions, above, and below—those who have been born into immeasurable pure Buddha-lands are beyond counting;
likewise, those who have become arhats and attained the path of nirvana are also beyond measure, such that they can no longer be calculated.

"The merit and virtue of the Buddha Amitābha are such that his acts of giving throughout the eight directions, above and below, are inexhaustible and infinite; they are profoundly deep, vast, and immeasurable, a sublime goodness beyond description."

The path of the sutras produced from the teachings of the wisdom of the Buddha Amitābha is proclaimed throughout the eight directions, above and below, to countless beings; in the heavens above and the world below, they are so numerous as to be beyond reckoning. The number of these sutra scrolls is vast and great, such that it can no longer be calculated—it is truly infinite.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Ajita:
"Do you wish to know the time of the infinite life of the Buddha Amitābha?
The Bodhisattva Ajita replied:
"I wish for all of you to hear and understand this.
The Buddha said,
"Listen attentively."

He caused all the devas, humans, and even the crawling and wriggling creatures throughout the countless Buddha-lands of the eight directions, above and below, to attain the human path; he caused them all to become *pratyekabuddhas* and *arhats*, sitting together in meditation with single-minded focus. They combined their wisdom into one courageous power, desiring collectively to calculate and know the immeasurable, pure lifespan of the Buddha—how many thousands of billions of *kalpas* and years it lasted—but none among them were able to calculate or know the ultimate, immeasurable lifespan of that Pure Buddha.
The Buddha said:

“Furthermore, suppose all the devas, humans, and even the crawling and flying insects within the Buddha-lands of a thousand Mount Sumerus in each of the other directions were to attain the human path; and suppose they were all made into pratyekabuddhas and arhats, all sitting in meditation with single-minded focus, and their wisdom were combined into one great vigor. Even if they wished to count the bodhisattvas and arhats in an immeasurable, pure Buddha-land—numbering in the hundreds of billions—they would be unable to count them.”
The Buddha said:
"The lifespan of the Buddha Amitābha is exceedingly long and vast; its illumination is immense and profoundly sublime, reaching to the infinite and the bottomless."
"Who would be able to believe and know this?
Only the Buddha knows it himself.
When Bodhisattva Ajita heard these words of the Buddha, he was filled with great joy; kneeling on his right knee with palms joined, he said:
“The Buddha has said that the lifespan of the Buddha Amitābha is exceedingly long, his majestic spiritual power is great, and his wisdom and radiance are lofty, sublime, and excellent.
Is he alone thus?”
The Buddha said:

“When the Buddha Amitābha finally enters parinirvāṇa, that Bhalluka Bodhisattva shall then become a Buddha, presiding over the wisdom of the Way and acting as the master of instruction for the world in the eight directions, above and below. All the devas, humans, and the myriad classes of crawling and flying creatures whom he delivers shall all be caused to attain the path of the Buddha’s nirvāṇa.”

His meritorious virtue shall cause him to become like the Great Teacher, the Buddha Immeasurable Purity, remaining for incalculable kalpas, incalculable kalpas, uncountable kalpas, and uncountable kalpas; following the Dharma, he shall only then enter parinirvāṇa.

"Next, the Bodhisattva Mahānāman shall become a Buddha; presiding over wisdom and presiding over all instruction, the merit of those he delivers shall be equal to that of the Great Teacher, the Buddha Immeasurable Purity (Amitābha). He shall abide for incalculable kalpas and shall never again enter parinirvāṇa."

Transmitted from one to another in succession, the reception of the sutras and the Way is exceedingly clear; the land is most excellent, and its Dharma is such that it shall never be severed and can never be exhausted.
Ānanda knelt with palms joined and asked the Buddha:

"The Buddha has said that in the land of the Buddha Immeasurable Pure Light there is no Mount Sumeru; upon what, then, do the first, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the second, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, rely for their dwelling?"
"I wish to hear it.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you have any doubts regarding the Buddha?"

Throughout the eight directions, above and below, there is no end, no limit, and no boundary. Even if a single person were to take up all the waters of the great oceans beneath these heavens and measure them out, they might yet be exhausted and their bottom reached;
the Buddha’s wisdom is likewise thus—throughout the eight directions, above and below, it is infinite, limitless, and without boundary.
The Buddha said:

"According to what I know and see through my wisdom, those Buddhas of the past whose names were Śākyamuni Buddha, just like mine, were as numerous as the grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges River—one Buddha for every single grain of sand."

Those who have recently come seeking to attain Buddhahood, such as myself, Śākyamuni Buddha, are as numerous as the grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges River—one Buddha for every single grain of sand.

The Buddha sat upright facing directly south; looking toward the south, he saw the Buddhas currently existing there whose names were identical to his own—Śākyamuni Buddha—as numerous as the grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges River, with one Buddha for every grain of sand.

In the eight directions, above and below, throughout the past, future, and present, all the Buddhas whose names are Śākyamuni Buddha—as many as the grains of sand along the banks of ten Ganges Rivers, with one Buddha for each grain of sand—[are likewise present].
"The number is thus; the Buddha has foreseen and known them all.
The Buddha said:

"Since incalculable kalpas in the distant past—whether one kalpa, ten kalpas, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, ten thousand kalpas, a hundred million kalpas, ten billion kalpas, or a hundred trillion kalpas—there have been Buddhas within these kalpas."

Regarding all the Buddhas who have already passed away—whether one Buddha, ten Buddhas, a hundred Buddhas, a thousand Buddhas, ten thousand Buddhas, a hundred million Buddhas, or a billion Buddhas—among them, each Buddha has his own name, and these names are not of a similar class; there is none that is identical to my name.

At the very beginning of the future eons, regarding all the Buddhas who will appear: in one eon, ten eons, a hundred eons, a thousand eons, ten thousand eons, a hundred million eons, ten billion eons, or a hundred trillion eons—within these eons there may be one Buddha, ten Buddhas, a hundred Buddhas, a thousand Buddhas, ten thousand Buddhas, ten billion Buddhas, or a hundred trillion Buddhas. Among them, each Buddha has their own name; their names are distinct and differ from the names of other Buddhas. Only at rare intervals does there appear a single Buddha whose name is the same as mine, Śākyamuni Buddha.

In all the eight directions, above and below, there are currently Buddhas in countless Buddha-lands. Beyond those, there are other Buddha-lands: one Buddha-land, ten Buddha-lands, a hundred Buddha-lands, a thousand Buddha-lands, ten thousand Buddha-lands, a hundred million Buddha-lands, ten billion Buddha-lands, and a hundred trillion Buddha-lands. Within these Buddha-lands there are Buddhas, each having their own names; these names are diverse and numerous, differing from one another and not being the same, and none of them bear the same name as mine.
Among the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above, and below, there is only one such as I, named Śākyamuni Buddha, appearing from time to time.
Throughout the eight directions, above, and below—encompassing the past, future, and present—the space between them is vast, desolate, and exceedingly remote, being infinite and boundless.

The Buddha’s wisdom is vast and exceedingly clear; he discerns the past to know the present. His foresight is infinite, his vision of the future is unimpeded, and his prophetic knowledge is boundless. He knows all the Buddhas—whose number is truly immeasurable and incalculable—through their majestic spiritual power and supreme brilliance.

The Buddha’s wisdom and moral virtue are united in brilliance; there is no one at all capable of questioning the Buddha regarding the ultimate depths of the sutras and the Way. The Buddha’s wisdom can never be measured or exhausted by a single measure.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, Ānanda was seized with great terror and his hair stood on end. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I do not dare to harbor any doubt regarding the Buddha.”

The reason I ask the Buddha is that in all the Buddha-lands of other directions there are Mount Sumerus, upon which the first, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, and the second, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, both depend for their dwelling.

I fear that after the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, there may be devas, humans, or members of the monastic community—whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—who come to question me: "Why does the Land of Immeasurable Purity of the Buddha alone lack Mount Sumeru?"
Upon what do the first, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, and the second, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, depend for their abiding?
I ought to answer this.
If I do not now ask the Buddha, after his passing what words shall I hold to give as an answer?
"Only the Buddha knows it himself; among all other people, there is none who can explain it.
For this reason, I am asking the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"If that is so, upon what causes and conditions do the third Yama Heaven, the fourth Tuṣita Heaven, and those above up to the seventh Brahmā Heaven depend for their dwelling?"
Ānanda said,
"These devas all dwell spontaneously in mid-air, without any support or cause.
The Buddha said:

"It is likewise in the Buddha-land of Immeasurable Purity that there is no Mount Sumeru; the First Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Second Trāyastriṃśa Heaven both abide spontaneously in mid-air, without any support or cause."
The Buddha said:
"The Buddha’s majestic spiritual power is exceedingly profound; he acts with sovereign mastery according to his will, and whatever he intends to do does not require prior calculation.

These various devas all constantly dwell naturally in the midst of space; how much more so is this true for the Buddha, whose majestic spiritual power is honored and who acts with sovereign mastery according to his will?"
When Ānanda heard the Buddha’s words, he was filled with great joy; kneeling with palms joined, he said:

“The Buddha’s wisdom knows the affairs of the eight directions, above and below, past, future, and present—boundless, infinite, and without limit. It is most lofty, vast, wondrous, and transcendent; it is delightful, excellent, and supremely luminous; it is marvelous beyond compare, and its majestic power is so venerable that it cannot be resisted.”
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Ajita:

"Among the people of the world—whether they be good men or good women—who wish to be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity, there are three grades; because their cultivation of merit varies in magnitude, they cannot reach one another."
The Buddha said:
"What are the three classes?

The most excellent and foremost class consists of those who leave home, abandon their wives and children, sever their cravings and desires, and practice as śramaṇas to attain the path of the unconditioned; they shall cultivate the bodhisattva path and practice the sūtras of the six pāramitās."

One who has become a śramaṇa should not fail or neglect the sūtras and precepts; one should practice with a compassionate mind and diligence, never becoming angry, and never engaging in sexual intercourse with women.

Maintaining the purity of the fast and precepts, with a mind free from greed or longing, one should aspire with the utmost sincerity to be born in the immeasurable, pure Buddha-lands, constantly maintaining this mindfulness without interruption.
When that person seeks the Way in this present life, they will see, within their own dreams while sleeping, the Buddha Amitābha and his various bodhisattvas and arhats.

When that person’s life is about to end, the Buddha Amitābha will personally come to meet them, flying through the air together with his bodhisattvas and arhats. They will then be reborn in the Land of Utmost Bliss, the Buddha-field of Amitābha, where they will be born by transformation within a lotus flower in a pool of the seven treasures; there, their bodies will naturally grow to full maturity.
Then, having become an avaivartika bodhisattva, he shall fly together with the ranks of other bodhisattvas to make offerings to the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above, and below.

Then, possessing wisdom and valor, they delight in hearing the sutras and the Way, their hearts filled with joy; their dwellings of the seven treasures abide in mid-air, where they may act as they wish according to their inclinations, remaining close to immeasurable, pure Buddhas.
The Buddha said:

"Those who wish to be born in the Land of Immeasurable Purity and who, with diligence, uphold the sutras and precepts and practice such supreme dharmas as these, shall be born in the Land of Immeasurable Purity and will be honored by the multitude; these constitute the foremost and highest class."
The Buddha said:

"As for those of the middle grade, these are persons who wish to be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity and Clarity. Although they are unable to leave their homes, abandon their wives and children, sever their desires, and become śramaṇas, they should uphold the sutras and precepts without fail, frequently practice the giving of alms, always believe and accept the Buddha’s words, and cultivate profound sincerity and loyalty."
Those who provide meals for śramaṇas, and who construct Buddhist temples, erect stūpas, burn incense, scatter flowers, light lamps, and hang various silk banners—such as these are the dharmas.

One should not harbor greed toward anything, nor should one give way to anger; maintaining the purity of the precepts and fasts, one should cultivate a compassionate mind with diligence and sever all thoughts of desire.

If one wishes to be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity and does not cease this practice for even a single day or night, that person will, in this very life, see the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity even within dreams while sleeping.

When that person’s lifespan is about to end, the Buddha Amitābha will manifest a transformation such that the person sees for themselves the Buddha Amitābha and his land; those who are reborn in the land of the Buddha Amitābha shall attain wisdom and valor.
The Buddha said:

"If a person practices giving in this manner, yet later feels regret and harbors doubts in their heart—disbelieving that the practice of *dāna* (almsgiving) and the performance of various good deeds will yield blessings in future lives; disbelieving in the existence of immeasurable, pure Buddha-lands; and disbelieving in rebirth within those lands—even so, if that person continues to maintain their mindfulness without interruption, though they may momentarily believe and momentarily disbelieve, remaining hesitant and lacking firm resolve, yet persists in binding themselves to their virtuous vows, they are called one who 'originally continues to attain rebirth.'"

When that person’s life span comes to an end and they are on the verge of death, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity will personally manifest a transformed image so that the person may see it with their own eyes. Though they can no longer speak, they will feel great joy and exultation in their heart, thinking to themselves:
"I regret not having known to increase my observance of the fasts and perform good deeds; now I shall be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity."
That person then repents within their heart; by repenting, their transgressions are diminished and they no longer require further atonement.

When that person’s lifespan comes to an end, they will be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity. Although they cannot yet reach the presence of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, they see on the way, at the edge of the realm of the Land of Immeasurable Purity, a spontaneously manifested city made of the seven treasures, and their heart is filled with great joy.

If one halts on the Path within that city, one will be born by transformation amidst lotuses in a pond of the seven treasures; there, one’s body will naturally grow to full size, and one shall remain within the city for five hundred years.

The city is two thousand li in both length and breadth. Within the city there are also dwellings made of the seven treasures; within these dwellings, both inside and out, there are bathing pools made of the seven treasures that appear spontaneously. These bathing pools are also naturally surrounded by flowers, and above the pools are rows of seven-treasure trees, all of which produce the sounds of the five musical notes.
When it was time for food and drink, there were naturally appearing meals before them, consisting of a hundred flavors, which they could obtain whenever they desired.

Those people lived in happiness within that city; the city was like the spontaneously produced objects of the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Yet those people could not leave the city, nor could they see the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity; they could only see his radiance, which caused them to feel self-reproach in their hearts and to leap with joy.

Furthermore, they will be unable to hear the sutras, nor will they be able to see the community of bhikṣus; nor will they be able to perceive or know the physical appearances and characteristics of the bodhisattvas and arhats within the immeasurable, pure buddha-fields.
If that person were merely to act in such a manner for a brief moment, the Buddha would not cause it to be so.
All that the body does is spontaneously attained; the mind itself naturally inclines toward the Way and enters its city.

When that person originally sought the Way in past lives, their mind and speech were at variance; their words and thoughts lacked sincerity, they harbored doubts regarding the Buddhist scriptures, and furthermore, they did not have faith or inclination toward them. Consequently, they will naturally fall into the evil realms.
The Buddha Amitābha took pity on him and, through his majestic spiritual power, led him away.

After five hundred years within that city, the man finally emerged and went to the presence of the Buddha Amitābha to hear the sutras; yet his mind did not attain understanding, nor was he permitted to listen to the sutras among the assembly of bodhisattvas, arhats, and bhikṣus.
Because they remain in their current dwellings and houses on the ground, they cannot cause those dwellings and houses to become as high or large as they wish or to be situated in the void;
furthermore, because they are immeasurably and extremely far from the Buddha Amitābha, they are unable to draw near to him.
That person’s wisdom is not clear and their knowledge of the sutras is meager; thus, their mind finds no joy and their intellect is not liberated.

After a long time, however, that person will naturally attain clarity of wisdom and knowledge of the sutras; becoming bright, vigorous, and courageous, their mind shall find joy, and they will subsequently become like the foremost group mentioned above.

Why is this? It is because that person, while seeking the Way during their previous lives, did not strictly observe the fasts and precepts; they violated the sutras and the Dharma, their minds were filled with doubt, and they did not believe the Buddha’s words. They did not believe in the profundity of the Buddhist scriptures, nor did they believe that by practicing *dāna* (generosity) and performing good deeds, one shall obtain blessings in future lives. Furthermore, they harbored regrets in the midst of their practice and did not believe in rebirth in the Land of Immeasurable Purity. Their cultivation of virtue was not performed with a sincere heart; for these reasons, they constitute the second grade of the Middle Class.
The Buddha said:

"As for those of the third grade, these people wish to be born in the Land of Immeasurable Purity. Even if they have no means to practice *dāna* (generous giving), nor can they burn incense, scatter flowers, light lamps, hang silk banners, construct Buddhist temples, erect stupas, or provide food and drink to the *śramaṇas*, they should sever their craving and desire, remain free from greed and longing, cultivate a heart of loving-kindness and diligence, refrain from anger, and maintain the purity of their precepts."

One who is thus pure should single-mindedly aspire to be born in the Land of Immeasurable Purity; if they do not cease for ten days and nights, at the end of their life they will be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity, where they shall attain supreme honor and possess courageous wisdom.
The Buddha said:

"After that person has performed these deeds, if they subsequently feel regret and harbor doubts—disbelieving that by performing good deeds one will obtain blessings in future lives, or disbelieving in rebirth in the Land of Immeasurable Purity and Clarity—that person, despite such thoughts, shall still continue to attain rebirth there."

When that person’s life is near its end and they are on the verge of death, the Buddha Amitābha causes them to see the land of the Buddha Amitābha within a dream while they are lying down and asleep. The person’s heart is filled with joy, and they think to themselves:
"I regret not having known to cultivate more merit; now I shall be born in the land of the Buddha Amitābha."
That person merely thinks this in their mind and can no longer speak it aloud; they then repent of their transgression.
For one who repents, the transgression is diminished and lessened; for one who repents, there is nothing further to reach [the consequences].

When that person’s life ends, they will be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity; however, unable to reach it directly, they see along the way a city of seven treasures extending for two thousand li. Their heart is filled with singular joy, and they settle within it.
Furthermore, they are born by transformation within lotuses in ponds made of the seven treasures, where they naturally grow to maturity.
Their city is also like the aforementioned cities, with natural objects comparable to those found in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa.

That person likewise remains within the city for five hundred years; when those five hundred years have ended, he finally emerges and arrives at the presence of the Buddha Immeasurable Purity, his heart filled with great joy.
When that person hears the sutra, their mind does not open to understanding, their heart does not rejoice, and their wisdom is not clarified; they possess little knowledge of the sutra.
Just as the house in which they dwell rests upon the ground and cannot be made tall or high at will to reside in the void of space, so too is it with the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity.

"As for the second class of those who harbor doubts, after a long time their wisdom shall also open and they will come to understand the sutras; with a courageous mind, they shall experience joy, becoming next in rank to the first class mentioned above."

Why is this so? It is because in their past lives, while seeking the Way, they were filled with regret and doubt; they believed for a moment and then did not believe for a moment. They did not believe that performing good deeds would later yield blessings and virtues, yet they all naturally obtained them nonetheless.

According to their respective merits, those who possess the handle and those who do not each naturally proceed toward their own course; their preaching of the sutras, their practice of the Way, and their eminent virtues are ten thousandfold and diverse, surpassing one another beyond reach.
The Buddha said, “Those who wish to seek the Bodhisattva path and be born in immeasurable, pure Buddha-lands shall all subsequently attain the stage of an Avaivartika Bodhisattva.”
Those who are *avaivartika* bodhisattvas shall all possess the thirty-two marks and the golden hue of refined purple, as well as the eighty secondary characteristics;

they shall all become Buddhas. According to their own aspirations, wherever they wish to become Buddhas in any buddha-field, they shall never again fall into the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts (*preta*).
According to one's diligent pursuit of the Way, whether it be morning or evening, every matter is equal;
if one seeks the Way without ceasing, one will surely attain it and shall not fail to realize one's aspirations and vows.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ajita and the assembly of devas, kings, and common people: "I tell you all:

those who wish to be born in the Immeasurable Pure Buddha-land, even if they are unable to practice great diligence, meditative concentration, or maintain the sutras and precepts, must nevertheless perform good deeds."

First, one must not kill living beings; second, one must not steal; third, one must not commit sexual misconduct by violating the wives of others; fourth, one must not engage in deceitful flattery; fifth, one must not drink intoxicants; sixth, one must not use double-tongued speech; seventh, one must not use harsh speech; eighth, one must not speak falsehoods; ninth, one must not be envious; tenth, one must not harbor covetous desires, nor be stingy in heart, nor prone to anger, nor mired in delusion, nor follow the whims of sensual cravings, nor feel regret in the heart, nor harbor doubt.

One should practice filial piety; one should practice utmost sincerity, loyalty, and trustworthiness; one should receive the profound words of the Buddha’s sutras; and one should believe that by performing good deeds, one will obtain their blessings in future lives.
Those who uphold this Dharma without deficiency or loss will, according to their aspirations, attain rebirth in the Land of Immeasurable Purity and Clarity.

It is essential that they observe the fast and precepts with single-minded purity, constantly contemplating rebirth in the Land of Immeasurable Purity and Clarity day and night for ten days and ten nights without interruption.
"I regard them all with compassion and shall cause them all to be born in the immeasurable, pure Buddha-lands.
The Buddha said:

"Those people in the world who desire to attain sagehood and clarity by practicing goodness while living at home as their path—dwelling together with wives and children, they remain preoccupied with the anxieties within the bonds of affection and desire."

If one has many household affairs and urgent duties such that there is no leisure for the great observance of precepts and single-minded purity, and although one cannot leave the home, one may, during times of leisure, rectify one's own mind, contemplate all manner of goodness, and practice the Way with focused diligence for ten days and ten nights.
Even if one is unable to do so, one should reflect and deliberate deeply:

"Those who wish to liberate themselves must, at the very least, sever discursive thoughts and cast off anxiety; they must not dwell on household affairs, nor share a bed with women. They should rectify their own body and mind, sever craving and desire, maintain the purity of the *upavāsa* fast with single-mindedness, and with focused intent, bring to mind the birth in immeasurable, pure Buddha-lands."

Those who do not cease [this practice] for even one day and one night will, at the end of their lives, all attain rebirth in that land; they shall be born by transformation within lotus flowers in bathing pools made of the seven treasures and shall obtain wisdom and valor.
The dwellings they inhabit will be houses made of the seven treasures, and they shall act according to their own free will, much like those of the first class mentioned above.
The Buddha spoke to the Bodhisattva Ajita:

"The countless devas, humans, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās from the eight directions, above and below, who are reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity—this great assembly shall all together gather at a bathing pool made of the seven treasures; each person shall sit upon a single great lotus flower and individually recount their own virtues and good deeds."

Each person spoke individually of their own past lives and destinies while seeking the Way: the sūtras and precepts they had upheld, the wholesome dharmas they had performed, the origins and details of where they had come from and been born, the sūtras and the Way they had delighted in, their wisdom regarding the sūtras, and the merits of the practices they had carried out; they recounted these matters in order from the highest to the lowest, until all had finished.

Because they know that the sutras have both clarity and obscurity, depth and shallowness, and greatness and smallness; because they naturally distinguish the excellence or inferiority, the thickness or thinness of virtues; and because they discern the vigor of their own talents and wisdom;

they observe one another’s marks with courtesy and harmony, all rejoicing and leaping for joy, their wisdom being courageous and fierce, yet each remaining independent and not seeking to surpass the other.
The Buddha said:
"That person did not previously cultivate merit with diligence; they were negligent in performing good deeds and lacked faith. Thus, they remained idle and indolent, acting in such a manner."
When the time came for the assembly to gather to discourse on the sutras and practice the Way, [the others] were naturally pressed by haste, and their responses were slow and delayed.
His wisdom of the Path was exceptionally distinguished and transcendent; his talent was marvelous, lofty, and fierce, while they alone were weak and emaciated at the periphery.
"To regret only when faced with the matter—once the regret has already emerged, what further benefit will it bring?
It merely results in a mind that is stubbornly attached to things like those [past objects].
The Buddha said:

"The assembly of bodhisattvas and arhats from the Land of Immeasurable Purity have all gathered together for this great dharma assembly. Restraining their minds and governing their intentions, they maintain upright bodies and correct conduct. They sport with profound mastery, flying together like banners in flight as they enter and exit, making boundless offerings with hearts full of joy and delight."
He delights in observing the sutras and practicing the Path, possessing harmonious and elegant literary refinement, as well as fierce talent and wisdom; his resolve is like empty space.
He seeks his vows with diligence, and his mind never again turns back midway, never again wavers, and never reaches a point of exhaustion.

Although one may appear slow and lax on the surface while seeking the Way, if within one is alone swift and urgent, remaining composed within the void, one will find the proper middle; with the inner and outer corresponding, one will naturally become dignified and orderly.

Restrained and upright, with body and mind pure and clean, they are free from craving and desire; they have no attachment or greed, nor do they possess any evils or defilements. Their aspirations are entirely stable and excellent, without increase or decrease.
Seeking the Way with harmony and rectitude, one does not err or fall into depravity; taking the Dharma as the standard and following the constraints of the sutras, one dares not violate or stumble.

If one moves within the lines of the compass and square throughout the eight directions, above and below, without limit or boundary, acting according to one's own will, one reaches the infinite and the boundless.

All together they take the Way as their practice, embracing its vastness and aspiring to its boundless expanse; they maintain a mindfulness of the Way that is free from other thoughts and devoid of anxiety or concern.
Spontaneously non-active and established in empty nothingness, they remain tranquil and desireless, cultivating virtue and making wholesome vows.

Exhausting one's heart in seeking and striving, harboring sorrow with compassionate pity, exerting diligence both inwardly and outwardly, and bringing ritual propriety and righteousness into perfect harmony;
penetrating all things without contradiction, being harmonious and submissive in accordance with the name, encompassing both the internal and external, and transcending to liberation.

Daringly ascending into *nirvāṇa*, one is forever united with the radiance of the Way and its Virtue; naturally maintaining and preserving this state, there is the overflowing joy of contentment. Truly and authentically pure and white, one’s aspirations are lofty and unsurpassed;
in pure concentration and profound stillness, the bliss experienced is without limit.
Excellent and beyond compare, its towering radiance shines brilliantly.
Once opened and attained, it is luminously penetrating; it is spontaneously the spontaneous characteristic, the fundamental source of spontaneity itself.

Spontaneously it forms five lights up to nine colors; these five lights up to nine colors revolve and circulate, undergoing hundreds of thousands of further transformations—the most supreme spontaneity.

The seven treasures are formed spontaneously; they span across to create the myriad things. Their radiant essence intermingles with the light, both emerging in beauty; their exquisite splendor is beyond limit.
Since the land of that realm is so exceedingly beautiful and fine as this, why do you not strive to do good?
"Mind the spontaneity of the Way, which is manifest in the absence of high or low; penetrate it without limits, and cast your will into the void.
Why do you not each exert yourselves with diligence to seek it for yourselves?"
One may transcend and depart, to be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity, the realm of Amitābha Buddha.
Crossing transversely through the five paths of existence, the evil realms naturally close off; ascending to the ultimate path, it is easy to go, yet few have reached it.
That land is free from opposition and follows the natural course.
Why not abandon worldly affairs to practice and seek the Way and its Virtue?
Thus one may attain ultimate longevity, with a lifespan and joy that are without limit.
"What is the use of worldly affairs? Why do you all share in this anxiety over that which is impermanent?
The people of this world are shallow and vulgar; they compete together over matters of no urgency.
Amidst such intense evil and extreme suffering, they exhaust their bodies to manage their livelihoods merely to provide for one another."

There is neither noble nor base, neither wealthy nor poor, neither old nor young, neither male nor female; all should together concern themselves with wealth and property, for whether one has it or not, the situation is the same.
Anxious thoughts are ever-present; one is filled with trepidation and suffering, burdened by constant reflections and deliberations that drive one to toil and service, finding no time of peace.

One worries about fields if one has fields, worries about houses if one has houses, worries about oxen if one has oxen, worries about horses if one has horses, worries about the six domestic animals if one has them, and worries about servants and slaves if one has them. Furthermore, one collectively worries over clothing, money, gold, silver, and precious objects.

Reflecting deeply with repeated sighs, one harbors grief and anxiety, fearing that one will be helplessly swept away, burned, bound, assaulted, or submerged by calamities, water, fire, thieves, enemies, or creditors; thus, the poison of sorrow and the state of agitation shall never find relief.

Bound by resentment, the heart harbors stifled breath and poisonous anger; the ailment resides in the chest and abdomen, such that sorrow and suffering never depart. The mind is firm and the will resolute, allowing for no relaxation or release.
Sometimes, while sitting in a state of self-destruction, one finally loses their life; having cast it aside and departed, there is no one who follows.
The noble, the wealthy, and the powerful possess such anxieties and fears, and endure such diligent suffering; they dwell together with the various afflictions of cold, heat, and pain.

As for those of humble means who are poor, destitute, and lacking, they too have their worries: having no fields, they worry about wanting fields; having no house, they worry about wanting a house; having no oxen, they worry about wanting oxen; having no horses, they worry about wanting horses; having no six domestic animals, they worry about wanting them; having no servants or slaves, they worry about wanting them; and having no clothing, money, utensils, or provisions for food and drink, they likewise worry about wanting these things.
Suppose there is one person who possesses little, and another who likewise possesses little; they both desire equality. When they have acquired a small amount, it is immediately exhausted.

Thus, suffering arises as they must again seek and search for more. Their thoughts bring no benefit, and they cannot obtain what they need in time; body and mind are both exhausted, and they find no peace whether sitting or rising.
Anxious thoughts follow one another, and their diligent suffering is such as this.
A burning mind does not leave them; resentment and solitary anger, as well as various chills, fevers, and pains, dwell together within them.
Sometimes one may sit [in meditation], yet end their life prematurely; they likewise refuse to do good or practice the Way.
When their lifespan is exhausted and they die, they must all depart alone into the distance, heading toward some destination, with no one able to know whether it be the path of good or evil.

"At times, among the people of this world—fathers and sons, brothers, husbands and wives, members of a household, and relatives by birth or marriage dwelling between heaven and earth—they ought to respect and love one another, and not harbor mutual hatred.
Regarding possessions, they should give to one another as needed and not be greedy.
Their speech and countenances should be harmonious; they must not oppose or contradict one another, nor should they contend in their hearts or give way to resentment and anger."
In this present life, even a slight sense of resentment, jealousy, or hatred leads to increasingly severe enmity in future lives. Why is this?

Because in this life one desires to harm another; though one does not immediately strike down or kill the other at that very moment, the sorrow, poison, and knots of indignation remain within the spirit. These naturally imprint upon consciousness and cannot be separated; thus, when reborn, they must encounter one another and inevitably seek retribution.

"While people in this world dwell amidst sensual desires, they come alone and depart alone; they die and are born alone, and as they travel toward their destined realms of suffering or pleasure, they must experience it themselves—there is no one who can take their place."

The transformations of good and evil, and the divergent destinations of calamity and retribution, await one in advance; when one must ascend alone and travel far to another realm, no one can see where one has gone.

Good and evil naturally follow one another into the next life; in the profound darkness of the afterlife, we are separated for a long time. Our paths diverge and there is no set time for meeting again; it is most difficult, most difficult to encounter one another once more.

Why not abandon all worldly affairs and, each of you, exert yourselves while in the strength of youth to strive diligently for what is good; by applying yourselves with vigor to transcend the world, you may attain the utmost longevity?
They are utterly unwilling to seek the Way; furthermore, what more could they wait for, and what could they possibly find joy in?

"In this way, worldly people do not believe that performing good deeds brings good results, they do not believe that practicing the Way leads to attaining the Way, they do not believe in rebirth in future lives after death, and they do not believe that giving alms yields merit and virtue—they do not believe in any of these things at all."

They also claim that this is not so, asserting that such a thing does not exist; yet, for this very reason, they merely observe themselves, looking at one another, and successively inherit the remaining instructions of their fathers.

One's ancestors and forefathers have not habitually performed good deeds and originally did not practice the Way; their persons were ignorant and their spirits dark, their minds obstructed and their intentions closed, such that they did not perceive the Way of Heaven. They were utterly incapable of seeing the births and deaths of human beings, nor could they know where they were headed, for they simply lacked the vision to discern the path of good and evil.

Furthermore, there is no such thing as speech; it is employed for the purpose of performing good or evil, merit or demerit, fortune or calamity, and each person competes to employ it for their own ends, yet there is nothing at all strange about this.

As for the path of birth and death, which revolves in continuous succession, turning upside down and back and forth, its root is impermanence; all such things must pass away and cannot be maintained forever.
Though taught and guided, those who believe in the Way are few, and all shall continue through birth and death without cessation.
Such people as these are blind and ignorant, obstinate and impulsive; they do not believe the words of the scriptures, each seeking only to gratify their own whims, their minds devoid of reflection.
They are foolish regarding sensual desires, ignorant of the Way and its Virtue, deluded by anger, and greedily attached to wealth and beauty.

If one sits [in meditation] yet fails to attain the Way, one must undergo further extreme toil and hardship; being reborn in evil realms, one can never find rest or peace—the pain of this is truly grievous.

"Sometimes, within a household—among father and son, brothers, or husband and wife—regarding the matter of life and death, they weep for one another and their mutual longing grows ever deeper. Their anxiety and resentment knot together as their bonds of affection continue to entwine; their hearts are so deeply pained that they gaze upon one another with constant thought, finding no moment of release day or night."

When moral instruction fails to enlighten the mind, and affectionate desires are not abandoned, one remains obstructed and muddled; with these conflicting states of delusion covering all, one is unable to reflect or deliberate.

If one’s mind is upright and resolute in dealing with worldly affairs, and one applies oneself single-mindedly to practicing the Path until the very end, yet fails to attain the Way when the span of one’s life comes to an end, there is nothing that can be done.

In general, all who are confused, clamorous, and contentious are driven by greed and desire; of those who follow such ways, many do not understand the Way while few attain it. The world is in a state of hurried bustle with nothing to rely upon;

noble and base, high and low, the wealthy and the poor, men and women, great and small, each busies themselves with their own affairs. They toil and strain their bodies, each harboring the poison of murderous intent; their evil vapors are dark and murky, and there is none who does not feel despondent.

They engage in reckless deeds that are rebellious toward Heaven and Earth; they do not follow a benevolent heart. Though their conduct is not inherently evil according to the Way and its Virtue, one first complies with them and allows them to act as they please.

Before their lifespan has even reached its end, they are suddenly snatched away and fall into the evil realms, where they endure toil and suffering for successive generations. They wander through cycles of grief and torment for many thousands of millions of years with no prospect of release; their pain is beyond words and they are truly to be pitied.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ajita and the assembly of devas, kings, and common people:
"I have told you all about the affairs of the world; it is because of these things that people remain seated and fail to attain the Way."

All of you should reflect upon this thoroughly: that which is evil you should let go of and distance yourselves from; that which is good you should firmly uphold. Do not recklessly commit what is wrong, but further cultivate all manner of goodness.
The glory of great or small, much or little desire can never be maintained; it must inevitably lead to separation and offers nothing to be truly delighted in.
During the Buddha’s lifetime, those who possessed faith and love for the profound Buddhist scriptures and who practiced the Way and its Virtue were all my younger brothers;
those who were just beginning to study the Buddhist scriptures and precepts were all my disciples.

Those who wish to leave their bodies behind, depart from the household life, renounce wife and children, and sever ties with wealth and beauty, coming forth to become śramaṇas and bhikṣus for the sake of the Buddha—all such persons are my sons and grandsons.
This world is extremely difficult to encounter; those who wish to be born in the immeasurable, pure Buddha-land shall attain wisdom and valor, and be honored by the multitude.
Do not follow your own whims and thereby fail or violate the sutras and precepts.
Should you find yourself lagging behind others and harbor doubts or fail to understand the sutras, come forward again and question the Buddha; the Buddha shall explain them for you.
The Bodhisattva Ajita knelt with palms joined and said:
"The Buddha’s majestic power is most venerable, and the sutras he has spoken are excellent and sublime.
As we have listened to the Buddha’s words, we have all contemplated them deeply in our hearts."
"The people of this world are indeed as the Buddha has said; there is no difference.

Now the Buddha, out of compassion for us, has opened our eyes to the Way of Heaven and taught us the path of rebirth. Our ears and eyes have become clear and sharp, and we shall forever attain liberation, as if having been born anew.
As we listen to the words of the Buddha’s sutras, there is none among us who does not feel a compassionate heart, rejoicing with leaping joy and attaining understanding."
We, as well as the devas, kings, common people, and even the crawling and flying insects—all have received the Buddha’s grace, such that none fail to attain liberation from sorrow and suffering.
The Buddha’s various teachings and precepts are profoundly deep, infinite, and bottomless.
That which is seen and known by the Buddha’s wisdom—regarding matters of the eight directions, above and below, past, future, and present—is unsurpassed and boundless.
"A Buddha is extremely difficult to encounter, and the Way of the Sūtras is extremely difficult to hear. We have all maintained hearts of loving-kindness toward the Buddha.
That we have now attained liberation is entirely due to the Buddha’s diligent study and his endurance of hardships while seeking the Way in previous lives."

His benevolence covers all universally; the merit and fortune resulting from his deeds are majestic and sublime; his radiance shines through with clarity, penetrating the infinite void, opening the way for entry into Nirvana.
