He teaches the sutras, establishing majestic discipline that transforms and pacifies all; his compassionate influence moves throughout the eight directions, above and below, without end or limit.
The Buddha is the supreme teacher and most honored of laws; among all sages, none can equal the Buddha.

The Buddha acts as a teacher for the devas, sovereigns, and people of the eight directions, above, and below; according to their respective inclinations and aspirations, he enables all, whether great or small, to attain the Way.

"Now that we have been able to meet the Buddha and hear the voice of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, we are filled with great joy; there is not one among us who has not attained wisdom and clarity."
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Ajita:
"What you say is true; it must indeed be so.

If there is one who possesses a heart of compassion toward the Buddha, they should truly and with great joy keep the Buddha in mind, for only after a long time in this world will another Buddha appear again."

Now, in this world of suffering, I have appeared as a Buddha to produce the Way of the Sūtras; I teach with thorough penetration, severing all doubts, straightening the mind and correcting conduct, uprooting all cravings and desires, cutting off the roots of all evils, walking without restraint, presiding over wisdom, encompassing the inner and outer aspects of all paths, grasping the fundamental principles, clearly and distinctly revealing the five destinies, and decisively establishing the path to birth-and-death and Nirvāṇa.
The Buddha said:

"For you all, from incalculable kalpas past—indeed, for kalpas beyond reckoning—you have practiced the path of the bodhisattva, desiring to deliver all devas, humans, and even the crawling and flying insects, for a time most remote and long ago. The number of people who have attained the Way and been delivered by you is immeasurable; those who have reached the state of nirvāṇa are likewise immeasurable."
You all, as well as the devas of the eight directions, above and below, kings, and common people—whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās.

All of you, since the beginningless kalpas of your past destiny, have transmigrated through these five realms of existence, wailing and lamenting at death and birth, weeping for one another, and harboring mutual greed and longing. Your anxieties, sorrows, and poisons have been such that their suffering is beyond description; thus, even unto this present life, birth and death have never ceased.
Now, on this very day, you have met with the Buddha and gathered together; encountering him, you hear the voice of the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, which is most refreshing.
Excellent! I assist you all in your joy, and you may likewise weary yourselves of the pain and itching of birth and death.

At the time of birth, it is extremely painful, extremely bitter, and extremely extreme; when one grows to adulthood, it is likewise bitter and extreme; at the time of death, it is likewise painful, bitter, and extreme. It is a place of extreme foul odor, utterly impure, and nothing about it is acceptable.

The Buddha therefore speaks to you all: you too may resolve for yourselves to eliminate the foulness and impurities of the body; you too may rectify your minds and align your conduct, diligently performing all manner of wholesome deeds. Thus, always maintain integrity both inwardly and outwardly, keep your bodies pure, wash away the defilements of the mind, exercise self-restraint, ensure that your inner thoughts and outer actions correspond, and be loyal and trustworthy in both speech and deed.

"If a person can liberate themselves and, in turn, assist others, uprooting all cravings and desires; with refined spirit and a sincere heart, their aspiration remains unshakable as they establish the foundation for the path of goodness."
Although diligent practice is arduous for a lifetime, it lasts but a brief moment.

By performing good deeds in this life, one will be reborn in the immeasurable, pure Buddha-lands of future lives, where joy is utterly boundless and one shall forever be united with the clarity of the Way.

Thus, they shall thoroughly preserve one another’s goodness, long remain free from the anxieties and afflictions of the evil realms, uproot the various evils that are the roots of suffering, and sever all cravings and attachments.

One shall attain eternal life in an immeasurable, pure Buddha-land, where there are no sensations of pain or itching, nor any place of foul odors; where there is no further hardship or suffering, nor any lust, anger, or delusion; and where there is no anxiety, worry, or the poison of grief.

"Born in the Land of Immeasurable Purity, you may wish for a lifespan of one kalpa, ten kalpas, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, or ten billion kalpas; it shall be granted according to your own will.
You may wish to abide for an incalculable number of kalpas or an uncountable number of kalpas; you may have your way and obtain whatever you desire."
Whether they wish to eat or not to eat, let their will be free; all things are spontaneously available and may be obtained.
Next, regarding the path to Nirvana, each shall individually and clearly seek it with vigor, according to what their hearts desire and vow.

Do not harbor doubts or feel regret in your heart; those who wish to be reborn there must not sit idly by their transgressions, for they shall be exiled for five hundred years within the city of the seven treasures at the edge of the Land of Immeasurable Purity and Clarity.
The Bodhisattva Ajita said:

"Having received the Buddha’s solemn and grave instruction, we shall all seek it with diligence and single-mindedness; we pray that you permit us to put it into practice, for we dare not entertain doubt or indolence."
The Sutra on the Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Three.
The Sutra on the Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Yuezhi Kingdom during the Later Han Dynasty.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ajita and the others:

"If you all, in this world, are able to restrain your own minds and rectify your intentions, and do no evil with your bodies, this shall be a great virtue and goodness, supreme and peerless throughout the eight directions, above and below."

Why is this? Because in the countless Buddha-lands throughout the eight directions, above and below, all devas and humans naturally perform wholesome deeds, do not commit great evils, and are easy to transform and instruct.
Now, as a Buddha in this world, I act as the most urgent savior amidst the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings.
I instruct the people to sever the five evils, to eliminate the five pains, and to cast off the five burnings;
I transform their minds so that they may uphold the five virtues, thereby attaining merit, transcending the world, and reaching the path of long life and Nirvana.
The Buddha said:
"What are the five evils?
What are the five sufferings?"
What are the five things that burn within?
What are the means for digesting the five evils and causing one to uphold the five virtues?
And what is the way to uphold the five virtues, thereby attaining merit, long life, transcendence of the world, and the path to Nirvāṇa?
The Buddha said:
"As for the first evil, it is when devas, humans, and even down to birds, beasts, and all classes of wriggling and crawling creatures desire to commit various evils."

"The strong subdue the weak, turning upon one another to harm and injure, devouring each other; they do not know how to do good, but act with wicked rebellion and unrighteousness, receiving their calamitous retribution as the natural course of the Way, toward which they must inevitably proceed."

The divine spirits record and remember [one's deeds]; transgressions are not forgiven, but continue to pass down through successive generations. Thus there are those who are impoverished, lowly, beggars, and solitary; those who are deaf, blind, mute, foolish, and depraved; and those of inferior status who are physically infirm, insane, or incapable.

Those who possess nobility and honor, great wealth, lofty talent and profound understanding, as well as wisdom and courage, all did so because in their past lives they practiced goodness, filial piety, compassion, and bestowed kindness and virtue.

Therefore, when there are official affairs, royal laws, and prisons, those who are unwilling to be cautious and refrain from committing evil will fall into the law; they undergo transgressions and reprimands, leading to severe punishments and extreme suffering, such that their hope for liberation is difficult to fulfill and escape is hard to attain.

In this world, the present is manifest; yet when life ends, the suffering becomes even more intense. Entering into the profound darkness and receiving another body for rebirth is like undergoing the most severe punishments under the laws of a king.

Therefore, there are those who naturally enter the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and the class of crawling and flying insects; they undergo the exchange of physical forms, transform their evils into the Way, and experience the varying lengths of their lifespans as their souls, spirits, and vital essences naturally proceed toward their destinies.

Having received a physical form and been entrusted with a womb, one must encounter [conditions] alone; yet beings arise together, turning back and forth to repay one another, and they must return to each other in turn.
As for calamities, evils, and punishments, as long as these manifold matters are not exhausted, one can never escape them.
Wandering through these realms, life after life across kalpas, there is no time of escape; liberation is difficult to attain, and the pain is beyond description.

Such things exist naturally within heaven and earth; though they do not arrive suddenly at a specific moment, they constantly follow the natural course of time. All deeds, whether good or evil, must return to their consequences—this constitutes one great evil, one great pain, and one great burning.
“Enduring such toil and suffering, lamenting with bitter grief, it is like a fierce fire breaking out and burning one’s body.

If a person can, amidst this, single-mindedly restrain their thoughts, maintain upright conduct, alone perform all manner of good deeds, and refrain from all evils, they shall alone attain liberation. They will obtain merit and long life, and cross over to the heavens above to attain the path of Nirvāṇa; this is the first great good.”
The Buddha said:

"As for the second evil, the world's emperors, officials, the people, fathers and sons, brothers, families, and husbands and wives lack even the slightest sense of righteousness and do not obey laws and commands."

They turn toward lust, extravagance, pride, and arrogance, each seeking to gratify their own desires and act according to their own whims. They deceive and manipulate one another, showing no fear of death.
Their hearts and mouths are at odds; their words and thoughts lack sincerity. They are sycophantic and disloyal, employing flattery and artful speech.
Their conduct was not upright; they harbored mutual jealousy and hatred, slandered one another, and fell into wickedness and injustice.
The sovereign was not enlightened and did not examine things with discernment; he relied upon his ministers, and thus these ministers came to exist [in power].
Those of shallow capacity may be able to act, yet they fail to discern the underlying circumstances; when those in authority are not upright, they become manipulated by others.

They recklessly cast aside the loyal and virtuous, failing to accord with the Will of Heaven and gravely violating the Way of Principle. Thus, ministers deceive their sovereigns, sons deceive their fathers, younger brothers deceive their elder brothers, and wives deceive their husbands.

Within and without the household, among kinsmen and acquaintances, each harbors greed and lust; their minds are individually filled with resentment and anger, shrouded in ignorance and folly, and their desires increase ever more.
Whether noble or base, superior or inferior, male or female, great or small, their minds are all alike in this regard: they seek only to enrich themselves.
They ruin their households and lose their lives, disregarding what lies before or behind them; because of them, their families and relatives suffer the destruction of their clans.

Sometimes those within and outside the household—acquaintances, friends, and the common folk of the villages and market towns—join together in these affairs, each seeking their own advantage at the expense of another.
They quarrel over wealth and money, becoming enemies through anger;
they further contend for victory and defeat, their hearts scorched by stinginess toward riches;
unwilling to give, they focus solely on guarding and hoarding.

Craving for precious things is heavy with greed; dwelling upon them in thought, the mind is exhausted and the body suffers. Thus it continues until the end, when there is nothing to rely upon; one comes alone and goes alone, with not a single person following.

Regarding good and evil, fortune and calamity, misfortune and punishment, and the destiny one pursues in rebirth—whether one dwells in a place of joy or enters into bitter suffering—one only then feels regret; once that has happened, what can be done? It will be too late.
"At times, there are those in the world whose minds are deluded and who possess little wisdom; seeing what is good, they slander and resent it, refusing to aspire to or follow it.
They desire only to do evil and recklessly commit unrighteous acts;
they desire only to steal and plunder, constantly harboring poisonous intentions."
Desiring to obtain the wealth and property of others to provide for oneself, one squanders it until it is exhausted, yet even after giving it away, one seeks it back again;

with a crooked and unrighteous mind, one is constantly and alone filled with terror, fearing that others perceive one's true nature; failing to exercise discernment when the moment arrives, one only regrets once the matter has already come to pass.
In the present life, officials and those in prison naturally fall into these states to undergo their misfortunes and retributions.
Those in this world who are impoverished, beggars, or solitary are so because of their past lives; they did not believe in the Way and its Virtue, nor were they willing to do good.

If one commits evil in this life, the celestial deities record it in their registers; at the end of one's lifespan, one enters the evil realms. Thus, there exist the natural hells (*niraya*), as well as the classes of birds and beasts, hungry ghosts (*preta*), and all kinds of crawling and flying insects.

Wandering through these realms from life to life for many kalpas, there is no time of escape; liberation is difficult to attain, and the pain is beyond description. These constitute the two great evils, the two pains, and the two burnings.
"To undergo such diligent toil is like being burned by a fire rising upon one's own body.

If a person can, amidst this, single-mindedly restrain their thoughts, maintain upright conduct, alone perform all manner of good deeds, and refrain from all evil, they will alone attain liberation. They shall obtain merit and long life, transcend the world to reach the heavens, and realize the path of Nirvāṇa; these are the two great virtues."
The Buddha said:

“As for those three evils: the people of the world exist as dependents upon one another, dwelling together between heaven and earth; yet regarding their years of life, none can endure for many years.”
Among them were those of noble rank and high status, as well as the wise and virtuous;
below were the poor, lowly, infirm, and foolish;

and in between were those of ill character who harbored only poisonous and evil thoughts, whose body and mind were not upright, and who constantly dwelt upon lustful excesses, which filled their chests with agitation.
Love and desire entwine, making one restless whether sitting or rising;
with a greedy mind and stingy attachment, one seeks only to obtain things for nothing;
casting sidelong glances at subtle forms, one displays wicked and licentious airs.

There was a wife who felt weary and loathing [of her husband]; she entered and exited at will and privately, took possession of the family's assets, conspired with others to commit wrongs, gathered for food and drink, and together they committed evil deeds.

They raise armies and act as bandits, besieging cities and engaging in combat; they commit robbery and slaughter, severing roads and blocking passages, using force to seize property in a manner contrary to the Way.
They steal and plunder for immediate gain, refusing to engage in honest livelihoods;
regarding what ought to be sought, they are unwilling to do it.
With an evil mind directed outward, he cannot act with focused intent;
wishing to strike and accomplish his ends, yet fearing the pressure of forceful intimidation, he takes what he has seized back to provide for his household.
Together they maintain their livelihood, indulging their hearts and seeking pleasure, exhausting their bodies in amusements, and committing adultery with the wives of others.

Or, regarding their own relatives, they show no regard for the distinctions of rank or seniority; the entire community comes to detest them, and both within and without the household, everyone suffers from and is distressed by them.

Furthermore, they do not fear government officials or the laws, showing no avoidance whatsoever. Such evils are recorded: naturally, they fall into prison; the sun and moon illuminate their consciousness, the divine spirits take note, and the various deities seize and register them.

"Therefore, there exist the natural hells, the realms of birds and beasts, the hungry ghosts (*preta*), and the wriggling insects and crawling creatures; transmigrating within these, through life after life and for many kalpas, there is no time of escape. It is difficult to attain liberation, and the suffering is beyond words. These are the three great evils, the three pains, and the three burnings. Such is the diligent toil and suffering, comparable to a fire breaking out that burns a person's body. If one can, amidst this, single-mindedly restrain the will, rectify the body and conduct, alone perform manifold good deeds, and refrain from manifold evils, then that person alone shall attain liberation. They shall obtain merit and virtue, achieve longevity, transcend the world, ascend to heaven, and realize the path of *nirvāṇa*. These are the three great virtues."
The Buddha said:

"As for those four evils, various wicked people are unable to perform good deeds; they bring about mutual ruin and destruction, and by instructing one another in turn, they collectively commit manifold evils."
The master incites others to speak, desiring only double-tongued speech, harsh words, reviling, and falsehood; they harbor mutual jealousy and engage in strife and discord.
They loathe and envy virtuous people, ruin the worthy and good, and take pleasure in evil when they see it in others.

Furthermore, they are unfilial and fail to provide for their parents; they treat their teachers, preceptors, and spiritual friends with contempt. Lacking faith, they find it difficult to attain sincerity.
Claiming for themselves that they are noble and possess the Way, they act with arrogant power and force, using their influence to oppress and exploit others without realizing their own faults.
Committing evil without any sense of shame or remorse, they are self-important and consider themselves quite capable, causing others to serve and revere them.

Furthermore, they do not stand in awe of Heaven and Earth, nor of the deities, nor of the sun and moon; they cannot be taught to do good, nor can they be transformed, for they remain stubbornly arrogant, claiming that such behavior is their constant way.
Furthermore, he felt no sorrow or grief, nor did he know fear; thus, he indulged in arrogance as he pleased. A celestial deity recognized him and thought:
"Fortunately, due to his past lives and karmic destiny, he has performed some merit; let a small amount of goodness support and sustain him, providing protection and assistance."

Having committed evil in this life, one's merit and fortune are utterly exhausted; all benevolent spirits and deities depart and leave one behind. Standing alone and empty, with nothing left upon which to rely, one undergoes heavy calamity and retribution.
As the end of one’s life approaches, evil pursues from behind; driven by natural necessity, one must hasten forward, unable to find rest.

Naturally, all manner of evils converge upon them, leaving them suddenly exhausted; their names are recorded in the registers of the divine spirits, and as their transgressions draw them along, they encounter their destined counterparts and must proceed toward their retribution.
Having undergone punishment and retribution, their bodies and minds are shattered; their spirits and forms suffer to the utmost, unable to escape, as they must press forward into the fiery cauldrons.
At such a time, what benefit would repentance bring?
What could possibly be achieved then?

"The Way of Heaven is spontaneous and allows no deviation; therefore, there are the realms of hell-beings, birds and beasts, hungry ghosts, and all classes of crawling and flying insects. One wanders through these states for successive lives and across kalpas, with no time of escape and liberation being difficult to attain. The pain is beyond description—this constitutes the four great evils, the four sufferings, and the four burnings."
"To undergo such diligent toil is like a fire breaking out that burns a person's body.

If one can, amidst this, unify the mind and control the will, keep the body upright and conduct right, performing many good deeds alone and committing no evil, then that person shall alone attain liberation, obtain merit and virtue, achieve long life, transcend the world, ascend to heaven, and reach the path of Nirvana; these are the four great virtues."
The Buddha said:

"As for those five evils, the people of the world loiter and are indolent; they are unwilling to do good and do not think of managing their livelihoods, so that their wives and children suffer from hunger and cold, as do their parents."
When he wished to reprimand and instruct his son, the son harbored ill will, glared with eyes full of rage, and spoke with discordant words.
His defiance and rebellion were worse than those of a common rustic; he was like an enemy. It would have been better not to have had such a son.

He borrows extensively and falsely from all, causing the multitude to suffer weariness and resentment; he is utterly devoid of gratitude and lacks any intention to repay his debts; when reduced to extreme poverty and destitution, he is unable to obtain anything further.

They compare their faults with a sense of rivalry, indulging in unrestrained wandering and dissipation. They have become habituated to obtaining wealth from the Tang and distribute it according to their own whims, showing no fear of prohibitions or restrictions.
Their consumption of food and drink knows no limit; they are addicted to wine and crave delicacies, and there is no fixed schedule for their comings and goings.
Rude and aggressive, he was ignorant of human feelings; with a haughty gaze, he forced others to submit.
Seeing someone rejoice, he would feel resentment, jealousy, and anger.
Devoid of righteousness or propriety, he acted solely according to his own will, deeming it his due right, and could not be admonished or enlightened.
Furthermore, they do not worry about whether their parents, wives, or children exist; nor do they think of repaying the virtue of their parents, nor do they think of the kindness of their teachers.
With a mind constantly harboring evil and speech constantly uttering evil, one achieves nothing throughout the day.

One does not believe in the Way and its Virtue; one does not believe in the existence of virtuous and enlightened sages of antiquity; one does not believe that practicing goodness constitutes the Way by which one may attain deliverance from the world; and one does not believe that there is a Buddha in this world.
They wish to kill arhats and incite strife among the community of bhikṣus; they constantly seek to kill people—desiring to kill their parents, brothers, wives, children, kinsmen, and friends.
Parents, brothers, wives, children, kinsmen, and friends detest seeing him and wish for his death.

He does not believe the words of the Buddhist scriptures; he does not believe that human life ends in death and is reborn in a future world; and he does not believe that performing good deeds brings good results, nor that committing evil deeds brings evil results.

“Such people—men and women alike—are of one mind in their contrariness and rebellion; they are shrouded in ignorance and delusion, filled with anger and lustful desires, and utterly devoid of discernment.”
They take their own self-willed pleasure and goodness to be great wisdom, yet they do not know whence they have come or where they shall go in birth and death.

They refuse to practice filial piety and act with such malice and rebellion against Heaven and Earth that they seek only luck and fortune within this state, desiring long life and personally attaining immortality.

They will inevitably return to the path of birth and death, toil and suffering, and good and evil; because of the evils committed by their own bodies, they will fall into the various realms of calamity and be unable to attain liberation.

Nor can they be subdued or transformed to lead them to do good; even when taught with compassion and guided through the transitions of birth and death and the destinations of good and evil, they still do not believe it.
Yet, though one exerts great effort and speaks with the desire to deliver them, it does not benefit those people.
Their minds remain blocked and their thoughts find no resolution; when their final hour approaches, they all feel regret at that time.
If one only regrets later, what can be done then?
If one does not plan for goodness in advance, what benefit will it bring when facing dire straits?
"Between heaven and earth, the five paths are distinct; vast and profound, immense and boundless, they pass on to one another in succession."
Good and evil, as well as poison and pain, one must experience personally; there is no one who can take their place.
This is the natural law of the Way: according to what one has done, one follows the destiny of rebirth, unable to abandon or evade it.
When good people practice goodness, they follow kindness, compassion, and filial piety; they enter from joy into joy, and from light into light.
When evil people practice evil, they enter from suffering into suffering, and from darkness into darkness.
Who is able to know this?
Only the Buddha knows and perceives it.
When he teaches and speaks to the people, those who believe and accept it are few; thus, birth and death do not cease, and the evil realms remain uninterrupted.

"Thus, it is impossible to fully describe the ways of the world; therefore, there are natural hells, as well as the realms of birds and beasts, hungry ghosts (*preta*), and all classes of crawling and flying insects. Within these, beings transmigrate from life to life through successive kalpas, with no time of emergence and no easy attainment of liberation. This suffering is beyond words. These are the five great evils, the five pains, and the five burnings."

"To undergo such diligent toil is like a fire breaking out that burns a person's body; yet if one can, amidst this, single-mindedly restrain the will, keep the body upright and conduct correct, ensure that words and deeds correspond, act with utmost sincerity, speak exactly as one says, let not the mind and mouth diverge, and alone perform manifold good deeds while refraining from manifold evils—then that person alone shall attain liberation, obtain merit and virtue, achieve longevity, transcend the world to reach the heavens, and realize the path of Nirvana. These are the five great virtues."
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ajita and the others:
"I have told you all that the five evils of this world involve such diligent suffering, giving rise to the five pains and the five burnings, which arise from one another in succession."

The people of the world are unwilling to do good and desire to commit various evils; should any dare to transgress these evil deeds, they will all naturally and inevitably pass through and enter the evil realms.
Or perhaps they have already been afflicted by the calamities of disease in this present life, yet they do not attain death; they manifest this for all to see.
When their lives end, they enter into the ultimate great suffering—agonizing, bitter, and cruel—and are themselves scorched, consuming one another until they are utterly extinguished.

Later, they became mutual enemies, harming and killing one another; from minor grievances arising to great and extreme calamities, it all stems from greed for wealth and beauty, refusing to practice patience and generosity, each desiring only their own pleasure, no longer distinguishing between right and wrong, seeking a reputation for prowess, driven by deluded desires, unable to attain what the mind imagines, with resentment festering within their chests.
Bound by wealth and sensual pleasures, they find no liberation; they know no contentment.
They enrich themselves while contending for desires, showing no self-reflection or restraint; they are utterly devoid of righteous principle and do not follow the True Path.

Wealth, nobility, and splendor may bring momentary gratification, yet if one cannot endure insults and does not know how to practice virtue, such power will last but a short while before being consumed by a foul reputation.
The body undergoes toil and hardship, which after a long time become exceedingly severe and follow one naturally, with no end in sight.
The laws of kings are spread abroad, naturally binding and raising up all;
superiors and subordinates correspond to one another, and within this net and its governing framework, one shall enter, trembling and anxious.
"Throughout past and present there have been such things; how painful and tragic!
The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Ajita and the others:

"If there be such Buddhas in the world, they will all feel compassion and pity for them, and by their majestic spiritual power, they will subdue and move away all evils, causing all such matters to be completely dissolved."
They cause them to abandon evil and turn toward the good, to cast aside their worldly thoughts, and to uphold the sutras and precepts, so that none fail to receive and honor them.

They practice the teachings of the sutras, not daring to violate or lose the path of world-transcending non-action and nirvana; this is a state of supreme goodness and ultimate bliss, profoundly luminous and infinite.
The Buddha said:

"If you—gods, emperors, kings, and common people, as well as those of future generations—encounter the words of the Buddha’s sutras, you should contemplate them thoroughly and be able to rectify your own minds and conduct accordingly."

The sovereign, practicing goodness himself, leads and transforms his subjects; he restrains those below him and instructs the people, exhorting them one to another to practice good together, to deliver one another, and to maintain their own integrity. They are compassionate and benevolent, remaining diligent until the end of life, honoring the sages and being filial, possessing profound and universal love.
The Buddha’s words and instructions must not be violated; one should be concerned with the path to nirvāṇa that transcends the world;
one should be concerned with severing birth-and-death and the sensations of pain and pleasure, thereby uprooting the foundation of evil;
one should be concerned with cutting off the paths of suffering for those in the hells, among animals, as hungry ghosts, or as the wriggling and crawling insects.
"When the Buddha is in the world, you must firmly uphold the Way of the sutras and not dare to lose it.
The Buddha said:
"If you all would practice goodness, what is the foremost priority?"

One should rectify one’s own body; one should rectify one’s own mind; one should rectify one’s own eyes; one should rectify one’s own ears; one should rectify one’s own nose; one should rectify one’s own mouth; one should rectify one’s own hands; and one should rectify one’s own feet.
One should be able to exercise self-restraint and refrain from acting recklessly; with body and mind pure and clean, one should remain in harmonious accord with what is wholesome.
Restraining both internally and externally, do not follow after cravings and desires, and do not commit any evil deeds.
One’s speech and appearance should always be harmonious, and one’s physical conduct should be focused; in walking, sitting, or rising, one should remain unmoving.

In whatever task one undertakes, one should first deliberate and calculate it thoroughly; one should assess one's own abilities and observe the proper method, then proceed with composure and slowness.
If one acts with haste, failing to plan in advance and performing the task without care, one will lose one's effort and suffer regret later, laboring in vain and bringing ruin upon oneself.
"Through utmost sincerity, loyalty, and faithfulness, one attains the Way and departs [from suffering].
The Buddha said:

"If you all cultivate various virtues therein, bestowing kindness and practicing merit, and are able not to sever the prohibitions of the Way—practicing patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom—and further transform and instruct one another, performing good deeds as acts of virtue."

If one practices this sutra-dharma with single-minded compassion and observes the pure precepts for a single day and night, it is superior to performing virtuous deeds for a hundred years in immeasurable, pure Buddha-lands.

Why is this? Because the Buddha-land of Immeasurable Pure Radiance is all accumulated merit and manifold goodness; it is unconditioned and spontaneous, such that whatever one seeks therein, there is not even a single evil as small as a hair.
The Buddha said:

"In this regard, one who performs wholesome deeds for ten days and ten nights shall obtain merit superior to that of the people in the Buddha-lands of other directions who perform wholesome deeds for a thousand years."

Why is this? In the Buddha-lands of other directions, all practice goodness; those who do good are many, while those who do evil are few. All things there are spontaneous; one does not need to strive for them, yet they are obtained of their own accord.
Here, however, those who do evil are many, while those who do good are few; if one does not strive, one cannot obtain anything.
It is simply because a person can rectify themselves, practice goodness, and seek the Way with a sincere heart that they are able to achieve this.
Within this world, there is nothing spontaneous; one cannot provide for oneself through mere chance, but must go forth to seek and diligently labor to sustain one's life.
They deceive and neglect one another, manipulating matters of good and evil; having obtained wealth and goods, they return them to provide for their wives and children.
They drink bitterness and consume poison, toiling their minds and exhausting their bodies; thus until the very end, their intentions are not focused, and their conduct remains restless and uneasy.
"If people can maintain inner tranquility and do good, and practice virtue with diligence, they are able to achieve this.

The Buddha said, "I have compassion for you all, as well as for the devas, kings, and the common people; I teach and command you all to perform various good deeds and refrain from all evils. According to each person's capacity, I immediately bestow upon them the Way, providing instruction and guidance that they should all faithfully carry out."

Thus, the ruler leads by example in transforming others through good instruction; ministers instruct their subordinates, fathers instruct their sons, elder brothers instruct their younger brothers, and husbands instruct their wives. Within the household, among kin and friends, they successively teach and exhort one another to practice goodness as the Way.

Reverently upholding the sutras and maintaining the precepts, each person remained steadfast and self-disciplined; superiors and subordinates restrained one another, whether noble or humble, male or female, all observing the fasts with purity and joy.
They harmonized with the principles of righteousness, encouraged one another toward compassion and filial piety, and mutually restrained themselves.

Whenever they encountered the words of the Buddha’s sutras, they would all uphold and contemplate them. They did not perform what should not be done; if they committed an offense, they would immediately repent their transgressions. They abandoned evil to pursue good and discarded the heterodox for the orthodox, reforming at evening what they had heard in the morning. They upheld the sutras and precepts with such intensity as a poor man who has discovered a treasure.

"Wherever the Buddha travels, in whatever commandery or kingdom he may be, he immediately bestows upon them the sutras and precepts. Then the devas, the sun, moon, and stars, the various spirits, kings, ministers, high officials, the populace, the nāgas, ghosts and spirits, those in the hells, and even birds and beasts all receive and practice them. Consequently, the ruler transforms his conduct to become virtuous; he observes the fasts and precepts with refined contemplation, purifies himself through ritual washing, aligns his mind and rectifies his actions, and maintains a solemn and reverent demeanor while occupying his station. He instructs and leads the masses toward goodness, upholds the prohibitions of the Way, and ensures that what is commanded is carried out and what is forbidden is ceased.
As for the ministers serving their sovereign, they are loyal and upright in receiving orders, not daring to disobey or betray them."

Fathers and sons shall speak with filial piety and obedience, receiving and upholding one another's instructions; brothers, spouses, kinsmen, and friends, as well as those of superior and inferior rank, shall command one another with compliant speech and harmonious reason. Those of high and low station, great and small, shall mutually respect and serve one another, acting with propriety and righteousness without mutual betrayal. None shall fail to reform their past and cultivate their future, purifying their hearts and transforming their conduct so that they are upright both inwardly and outwardly. Thus, they will naturally perform good deeds and obtain whatever they wish for immediately.

If one is moved by the Way of natural transformation through the cultivation of goodness, then if one seeks immortality, one may attain long life; if one seeks to transcend the world, one may attain the Way of Nirvāṇa.
The Buddha said:
"The majestic power of a Buddha is profound and venerable; it eliminates evil and transforms it into goodness, such that there is none who is not delivered and liberated.

Now I have appeared in the world, becoming a Buddha within this evil and suffering age. Out of compassion and pity, I instruct, exhort, and guide all devas, emperors, ministers and attendants, high officials, and the common people, causing them all to attain the Way according to their respective inclinations, vows, and aspirations."

In all places where the Buddha traveled—whether through provinces and kingdoms, towns and villages, hamlets and market towns—everything became abundant and fertile; the world was at peace, and the sun and moon shone with redoubled brilliance.
Winds and rains fell according to the seasons, and the people were tranquil and secure;
the strong did not oppress the weak, and each found their rightful place.

There shall be no years of famine or pestilence; none shall suffer from illness or emaciation; weapons of war shall not be raised; the land shall be free of thieves and bandits; there shall be no grievances or injustices; and none shall be subjected to imprisonment or confinement.

The ruler and his ministers, as well as the people, were all filled with joy; with loyalty, compassion, and utmost sincerity, each maintained their proper conduct. All naturally governed the state in harmony and filial obedience, and there was none who did not rejoice.

They shared both material goods and the bestowal of kindness and virtue; their hearts were joyful and they all held one another in mutual respect and affection. They deferred to one another’s wealth and yielded to righteousness, showing humility and yielding precedence.

Before and after, they served one another with ritual propriety, like father and son, like elder and younger brother; there were none who were not benevolent and worthy. In harmony and accord, they observed the rules of etiquette without any conflict or dispute, achieving an unsurpassed state of joy and goodness.
The Buddha said:
"I pity these children and wish to deliver them, caring for them even more than parents care for their own children.

Now, among the devas, emperors, and commoners of the eight directions and the zenith and nadir, as well as all classes of wriggling and crawling creatures, those who obtain the sutras and precepts of the Buddha and practice the Buddha-way shall all attain clear wisdom; their minds will be fully opened and understood, and there shall be none who do not transcend and escape from sorrow and suffering."

Now that I have become a Buddha and dwell amidst the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings, I subdue and transform the five evils, eliminate and exhaust the five pains, and utterly extinguish the five burnings. By using the good to counteract the evil, I uproot poisonous suffering and cause the five virtues to become bright and excellent, so that the burning of evil shall not arise again.

After my parinirvāṇa, the path of the Dharma will gradually be severed. People will become sycophantic and thoroughly commit various evils, no longer performing good deeds. The five fires will rise again, and the five agonizing pains will be more intense—occurring just as before—and they will naturally recur, becoming increasingly severe over time beyond what can be fully described; I have merely taught you this way of the lesser path.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ajita and the others:
“Each of you should contemplate and uphold this, and teach and admonish one another in turn, so that none dare transgress the Dharma of the Buddha’s sutras.”
The Bodhisattva Ajita knelt with palms joined and said:
"What the Buddha has spoken is most grievous; that the world’s people commit such extreme evils is indeed so, indeed so."
The Buddha, out of universal compassion, delivered them all; they all said,
"We receive the Buddha’s solemn instruction and request that it be passed down in succession," and they did not dare to violate it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Out of compassion for you all, I shall cause you to see the immeasurable, pure Buddha and the lands where the various bodhisattvas and arhats dwell."
"If you wish to see them?
Ānanda was greatly delighted; kneeling with palms joined, he said, "I wish to see them all."
The Buddha said:

"If you rise again, put on your kashaya robe, and face west—toward where the sun sets—to pay homage to the Buddha of Immeasurable Pure Radiance, prostrating with your head and face touching the ground, saying:
'Namo to the Buddha of Immeasurable Pure Radiance and Equal Enlightenment.'"
Ānanda replied, “Yes, I shall receive your instruction.

He then rose, adjusted his *kāṣāya*, and turned westward to bow toward the place where the sun had set that day. He paid homage to the Buddha Immeasurable Purity, placing his head upon the ground and saying:
"Homage to the Buddha of Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment.

Before Ānanda had risen, the Buddha of Immeasurable Pure Enlightenment emitted a great radiance of majestic spiritual power, which pervaded the countless buddha-lands in the eight directions, above, and below; the heavens and earth were all greatly shaken.

Throughout the countless worlds of the devas, the jeweled Mount Sumerus, the great jeweled Mount Mahāsumerus, and all the great and small world-systems—within which there were great and small hells, as well as mountains, forests, valleys, and dark, obscure places—all became brilliantly illuminated, and a great opening unfolded everywhere like falling rain.

Then Ānanda, the bodhisattvas, the arhats, and others, as well as the devas, kings, and the people, all beheld the Buddha Amitābha, the various bodhisattvas, the arhats, and the land of the seven treasures. Their hearts were filled with great joy and they leaped for gladness;
they all rose and paid homage to the Buddha Amitābha, touching their heads to the ground, and all exclaimed: “Namo Amitābha Samyaksambuddha!”

After the Buddha Amitābha had emitted his radiant light and majestic spiritual power, all the innumerable devas, humans, and even the crawling and flying insects beheld the radiance of the Buddha Amitābha; there was none who did not respond with a heart of compassion and joy, performing virtuous deeds.

All those in the hells, among the animals, or as hungry ghosts, and all those in places of rigorous punishment and diligent suffering, shall all find rest and no longer be tormented; there shall be none who are not liberated from their grief and pain.
All who were blind regained their sight; all who were lame, crippled, or infirm were able to walk and run; all who were ill were healed and rose up;

all who were weak became strong and healthy; the foolish all became more wise; those who were lustful or wrathful all came to act with a compassionate heart and do good; and for all who had been poisoned, the poison ceased to take effect.
The bells, drums, lutes, harps, *konghou* lutes, and all other musical instruments and performers produced sounds spontaneously without being struck;
the pearl bracelets of the women all made their own sounds;
and the hundred birds and beasts all cried out in lamentation on their own accord.
At that time, there were none who did not rejoice or attain deliverance.

On that very day, the devas and humans in the lands of all Buddhas took celestial flowers and incense and descended from the void, making offerings to all by scattering them upon the Buddhas and the Immeasurable Pure Buddha.
The various devas each together performed ten thousand kinds of spontaneous music, delighting the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas, and the Arhats.
At that time, the joy was so profound it was beyond words.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda, the Bodhisattva Ajita, and the others:
"When I speak of the Buddha Immeasurable Pure Light, his various bodhisattvas, arhats, and the land of natural seven treasures, would there not be no difference [between them]?"
Ānanda knelt with palms joined and said:
“The Buddha has described the land of the Buddha of Immeasurable Pure Radiance as blissful and excellent; it is exactly as the Buddha has spoken, without any difference.”
The Buddha said:

"I have been describing the immeasurable, pure, and meritorious land of the Buddha Amitābha for a day and night—an entire kalpa—and it is still not yet finished; I have merely given you a brief account."
The Bodhisattva Ajita then knelt with palms joined and asked the Buddha:
"From this world, how many *avaivartika* bodhisattvas will now be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity?"
"I wish to hear it.
The Buddha said,
"If you wish to know, listen attentively and take it to heart."
The Bodhisattva Ajita replied,
"I shall receive your instructions.
The Buddha said:

“From my land, seven hundred and twenty billion *avaivartika* bodhisattvas shall all be reborn in the Buddha-land of Immeasurable Purity—each of these *avaivartika* bodhisattvas having made offerings to countless Buddhas in succession and destined to attain Buddhahood just as Maitreya shall—and furthermore, an incalculable number of other minor bodhisattvas shall likewise all be reborn in the Buddha-land of Immeasurable Purity.”
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Ajita:
"Not only shall the bodhisattvas within my own land be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity, but there are likewise Buddhas in other lands and different realms who are exactly like this."
The first Buddha is named Guangyuanzhao (Light Shining Afar); in his land there are eighteen billion bodhisattvas who shall all be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity.
In another realm, a second Buddha, whose name is Baoji (Jewel Accumulation), has ninety billion bodhisattvas in his land who shall all be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity.
In another land, a third Buddha named Vimalabuddhi has two hundred and twenty billion bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
In another land, a fourth Buddha named Infinite Radiance resides; there are twenty-five billion bodhisattvas in that land who shall all be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity.
In another land, a fifth Buddha named Anuttara (Supreme in the World) resides; there are six hundred billion bodhisattvas in that land who shall all be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity.
In another land, a sixth Buddha named Vīraprabha resides; there are fourteen thousand bodhisattvas in his land who shall all be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity.
In another land, a seventh Buddha named Fully Endowed with Interlacing resides; fourteen billion bodhisattvas from that land shall all be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity.
In another land, a different country, there is an eighth Buddha named Śūramatirāja; in that land there are eight bodhisattvas who shall all be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity.

In another land, a different country, there is a ninth Buddha named Most Powerful and Unsurpassed; in that land, there are eight hundred and ten billion bodhisattvas who shall all be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity.
In another land, a tenth Buddha named Kṣema resides; in that country there are ten billion bodhisattvas who shall all be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity.
In another land, the eleventh Buddha is named Hui-bian (Wisdom Eloquence). In that land, there are twelve thousand bodhisattvas who shall all be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity.

In another land, a twelfth Buddha named Anuttara-puṣpa (Unsurpassed Flower) resides. In that land there are bodhisattvas, countless and beyond calculation—all of whom are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive), all of whom possess courageous wisdom, and each of whom has made offerings to countless Buddhas. With a single-minded aspiration to be born there, they shall all be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity (*Amitābha*).

In another land, a different country, there is a thirteenth Buddha named Great Joyful Wondrous Sound; in that land, there are seven hundred and ninety billion bodhisattvas who shall all be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity.
The Buddha said:
"These bodhisattvas—all of whom are *avaivartika*—along with the assembly of bhikṣus and countless junior bodhisattvas, shall all be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity."

Not only shall the bodhisattvas from the lands of these fourteen Buddhas be reborn there, but likewise all the bodhisattvas from the countless Buddha-lands throughout the eight directions, above and below, shall each and every one be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity.

They all gathered together in incalculable numbers, and the great assembly in the immeasurable, pure Buddha-lands was so vast as to be beyond reckoning; were I merely to recite the names of the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above, and below, it would not be finished even in a single kalpa of day and night.

If I were to further describe the number of bhikṣu saṃghas in the Buddha-lands and the number of bodhisattvas who shall be reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Purity, I would not finish even if I spoke for an entire kalpa without ceasing.
"I have merely summarized and briefly recounted this for you all.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, Ajita Bodhisattva, and the others:

"As for the world's kings, people, good men, and good women, the marks and fortunes resulting from the wholesome deeds they performed in their past lives enable them to hear the voice of the Buddha Amitābha; that they respond with a compassionate heart and joy—this I rejoice in on their behalf."
The Buddha said:

"If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who, upon hearing the name of the Buddha Immeasurable Purity, feel joy and compassion, leaping for joy all at once with pure hearts and their hair standing on end, they have all practiced the path to Buddhahood in their past lives—whether as Buddhas of other directions or as bodhisattvas, for they are certainly no ordinary persons."

As for those people—whether men or women—who hear the name of the Buddha Amitābha yet do not believe that there is a Buddha, do not believe the words of the Buddha’s sutras, do not believe that there is a Sangha of bhikṣus, and harbor doubts in their hearts such that they have no faith at all: these have all come from the evil realms. Born ignorant and unable to understand their past lives, their calamities and evils are not yet exhausted and they are not yet destined for liberation; therefore, they harbor doubts in their hearts and do not place their trust in him.
The Buddha said: "I tell you all:
whatever wholesome dharmas you ought to practice, you must all faithfully carry out and believe in them.
Do not, on account of my passing into parinirvāṇa, say that you or future generations may no longer [practice them]."
"I do not believe that there is a land of Immeasurable Purity and Clarity.
Therefore, I have caused you all to see this land of Immeasurable Purity and Clarity; as for what ought to be done, seek it yourselves.
I have fully expounded for you all the sutras, precepts, and the Dharma in accordance with the truth; you should uphold them as the Buddha’s teachings, and must not let them be lost or corrupted.
I entrust this sutra to you all; you should hold it fast and must not arbitrarily increase or diminish the Dharma of this sutra.

After my parinirvāṇa, the path of the scriptures shall remain for a thousand years; after those thousand years, the path of the scriptures will be severed, yet those who possess the aspiration in their hearts shall all be able to attain the Way.
The Buddha said:
"The teacher opens and guides the ears and eyes of others; his wisdom is clear and penetrating, and he delivers people so that they may attain goodness and enter the path of Nirvana."
"You should always be compassionate and filial toward the Buddha as you would toward your own parents;
you should constantly remember the kindness of your teachers, maintaining that mindfulness without interruption, and thus you shall swiftly attain the Way.
The Buddha said:

"It is extremely rare to encounter a Buddha in this world; it is also extremely rare to find a person who faithfully accepts the teachings and the profound words of the sutras; and it is extremely rare to find a śramaṇa or a teacher who expounds the Buddha’s sutras for others."
When the Buddha spoke this sutra, twelve trillion devas and humans all attained the divine eye of penetrating vision; with one mind, they all set out upon the path of the bodhisattva.
Furthermore, twenty-two billion devas and humans all attained the stage of anāgāmin, and eight hundred śramaṇas all attained the stage of arhat.
Then four billion bodhisattvas all attained the stage of *avaivartika*.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bodhisattvas, arhats, devas, kings, and common people were all greatly delighted. They came forward to pay homage to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and departed with their heads touching his feet.
The Sutra on the Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Four.
